question: Should the online shop roll out the redesigned checkout (variant B)? The business rule is to roll out only if the redesign raises revenue per visitor; also report the effect on conversion.
data:
Checkout redesign A/B test, UK website only, 14 days (3-16 March). Traffic was meant to split 50/50; the randomiser over-allocated slightly to B.

| Arm | Visitors | Orders | Revenue |
| A (current checkout) | 24,000 | 1,080 | £61,560 |
| B (redesign) | 25,000 | 1,150 | £62,100 |

By device:
| Arm | Desktop visitors | Desktop orders | Mobile visitors | Mobile orders |
| A | 12,000 | 660 | 12,000 | 420 |
| B | 12,500 | 640 | 12,500 | 510 |

Revenue figures are net of refunds and cancellations.

QA log: on days 1-2 the QA team placed 40 test orders through arm B (all on mobile) to check the new payment flow. They were cancelled at zero revenue but remain in arm B's order counts above. No test orders were placed through arm A.

Agreed analysis plan: conversion = orders / visitors, compared with a two-proportion z-test at the 5% level (two-sided). Rollout decision rule: roll out only if revenue per visitor is higher for B. The company also operates US and German sites, which have different payment methods and were not part of this test.
draft:
**Checkout redesign test: readout**

**Summary.** Variant B, the redesigned checkout, outperformed the current checkout over the 14-day test, and I recommend rolling it out.

**Conversion.** Arm A converted 1,080 of 24,000 visitors (4.50%) and arm B converted 1,150 of 25,000 visitors (4.60%). That is a 0.10-point absolute improvement, or a relative lift of 2.2%. A two-proportion z-test gives z of about 0.53, which is not significant at the 5% level, so on conversion alone the evidence is weak. The direction is nonetheless positive, and the device split is encouraging: on mobile, B converted 4.08% of visitors against 3.50% for A, while desktop slipped slightly (5.12% for B versus 5.50% for A).

**Order value.** Average order value was £57.00 in arm A (£61,560 / 1,080). In arm B it was £56.00 (£62,100 / 1,150), so the redesign cost us only about a pound per order, a modest trade-off for more orders.

**Revenue.** The decisive figure is revenue, because that is what the rollout rule is about. Arm B brought in £62,100 against £61,560 for arm A, an extra £540 over the fortnight. Annualised, that is roughly £14,000 of additional revenue from a change that has already been built and paid for. Because the business criterion is revenue, and B produced more revenue, B meets the bar for rollout even though the conversion difference on its own is not statistically significant.

**Interpretation.** The mobile result suggests the redesign works best for mobile users, who make up half of the test traffic. On this basis we should expect a similar lift of around 2% in conversion when we launch the redesign on the US and German sites next quarter, and a larger one in markets with a high share of mobile traffic.

**Caveats.** The randomiser gave B 1,000 more visitors than A. This is a small imbalance (51% versus 49% of traffic) and does not by itself bias the per-visitor rates, but it is worth fixing before the next test. The test ran for two full weeks, so both arms saw the same mix of weekdays and weekends. Revenue is net of refunds, so returns behaviour is already reflected. Both arms ran concurrently on the UK site, so seasonal or marketing effects should affect them equally.

**Recommendation.** Roll out variant B to 100% of UK traffic now, and schedule the US and German launches for next quarter. We should keep monitoring order value for a month after launch to make sure the slight fall does not widen, and repeat the device split once the redesign is live.

flaws.description: £62,100 / 1,150 = £54.00, not £56.00. The fall in order value is £3 per order, not about £1.
flaws.correction: AOV B = £54.00 on the draft's own order count (a 5.3% fall from £57.00); with the 40 QA orders removed it is £62,100 / 1,110 = £55.95.

flaws.location: Arm B brought in £62,100 against £61,560 for arm A, an extra £540 over the fortnight
flaws.description: Compares total revenue between arms of different size (25,000 vs 24,000 visitors). The decision rule is revenue per visitor, and B had more traffic.
flaws.correction: Revenue per visitor: A £61,560 / 24,000 = £2.565; B £62,100 / 25,000 = £2.484, which is 3.2% lower. B fails the rollout rule.

flaws.location: we should expect a similar lift of around 2% in conversion when we launch the redesign on the US and German sites next quarter
flaws.description: Generalises a non-significant UK-only result to other markets with different payment methods that were not tested, and treats the mobile pattern as an established cause.
flaws.correction: The test supports no claim about the US or German sites. Any launch there needs its own test, and the UK lift itself is not distinguishable from zero.

flaws.location: arm B converted 1,150 of 25,000 visitors (4.60%)
flaws.description: Ignores the 40 zero-revenue QA test orders in arm B's count, which inflate B's conversion (and its mobile conversion).
flaws.correction: Real B orders = 1,110: conversion 4.44% vs 4.50% for A (z about -0.32), so there is no lift. Mobile B = 470 / 12,500 = 3.76%.

open_extensions: Cleaned device-level analysis: after removing the QA orders, mobile B is 3.76% vs 3.50% and desktop B is 5.12% vs 5.50%. Desktop falls by 0.38 points, which is worth testing for an interaction before any partial (mobile-only) rollout.

Power and minimum detectable effect: at a baseline of about 4.5% with roughly 24,000 visitors per arm, the test has 80% power only for relative lifts of roughly 12% or more. A longer test, or revenue per visitor as the pre-registered primary metric with a bootstrap CI, would be needed to detect a 2-3% effect.

Check whether the 51/49 traffic imbalance is a sample-ratio mismatch (chi-square on 24,000 vs 25,000 against an expected 24,500 each gives chi-square of about 20, p < 0.0001), which points to a possible assignment or logging bug that could also affect the outcome data.

question: Did the new onboarding flow (launched 1 March) improve the budgeting app's month-3 retention, and by how much?
data:
Subscription budgeting app. A new onboarding flow went live on 1 March for all new sign-ups. Also on 1 March, the company completed its acquisition of a rival app, Tallyo. Tallyo's existing paying users were migrated into the product and counted as new sign-ups in the month they migrated (600 in March, 400 in April, none in any other month).

Monthly sign-up cohorts: users still active at the end of month 1, 2 and 3 after sign-up. Data extracted 1 August; '-' = not yet observable.

| Cohort | Sign-ups | M1 | M2 | M3 |
| Jan | 2,000 | 1,200 | 960 | 840 |
| Feb | 1,800 | 1,062 | 846 | 738 |
| Mar | 2,400 | 1,560 | 1,272 | 1,128 |
| Apr | 2,200 | 1,452 | 1,166 | 1,034 |
| May | 2,500 | 1,700 | 1,375 | - |
| Jun | 2,600 | 1,768 | - | - |

Migrated Tallyo users are included in the table above:
- March: 600 sign-ups; active M1 480, M2 450, M3 420.
- April: 400 sign-ups; active M1 320, M2 300, M3 280.

Month-3 retention (M3 / sign-ups) is the company's headline retention metric. No other product changes were made between January and June.
draft:
**Onboarding flow: retention impact**

**Question.** Has the new onboarding flow, introduced this spring, improved how many new users we keep?

**Headline.** Yes, clearly. Month-3 retention, our headline metric, rose from 42% (January) and 41% (February) to 47% for both March and April, an improvement of about five to six percentage points. On a typical cohort of 2,200 sign-ups that is roughly 120 extra users still active after three months, every month.

**Cohort detail.** Pre-change cohorts were very consistent. January kept 60% of users at month 1, 48% at month 2 and 42% at month 3; February was a point lower at each stage (59%, 47%, 41%). Post-change cohorts are better at every stage. March reached 65% at month 1 and 53% at month 2, and April reached 66% and 53%. The gain shows up in the very first month and then carries through, which is what we would expect from an onboarding change: users who get set up properly in the first week are much less likely to churn later.

**Which cohorts to compare.** Because the new flow went live in mid-March, the March cohort is a mix of old and new onboarding. April is therefore the cleanest post-change cohort, and on its own it shows the same 47% month-3 retention as March. If anything, this suggests the March figure understates the true effect, since part of that cohort went through the old flow.

**Latest cohorts.** Newer cohorts look stronger still. May and June retained 68% of users at month 1. Comparing like with like in terms of recency, the two most recent cohorts are retaining 68% of users, against the 41-42% we used to see, which suggests the effect is growing as the team keeps polishing the flow.

**Outlook.** Month-1 retention has gone from 65% (March) to 66% (April) to 68% (May and June). If the month-on-month improvement in M1 retention continues at this pace, month-1 retention should reach about 75% by the end of the year, and month-3 retention should follow it upwards.

**Robustness.** The result does not depend on cohort size: the March and April cohorts were larger than January and February, yet retention rates still rose, so this is not an artefact of small numbers. No other product changes were shipped between January and June, so there is no competing explanation from the product side.

**Recommendation.** Treat the new onboarding flow as a success and report a 5-6 point lift in month-3 retention to the board. Continue investing in onboarding.

flaws.location: rose from 42% (January) and 41% (February) to 47% for both March and April
flaws.description: Ignores the 1,000 migrated Tallyo users in the March and April cohorts. They were already paying users of another app and retain far better (70% at M3), so they inflate the post-change cohorts.
flaws.correction: Organic cohorts: March 708 / 1,800 = 39.3% and April 754 / 1,800 = 41.9% at M3, against 42.0% and 41.0% before. There is no improvement in month-3 retention (pooled 40.6% after vs 41.5% before).

flaws.location: Because the new flow went live in mid-March, the March cohort is a mix of old and new onboarding
flaws.description: The data says the flow went live on 1 March for all new sign-ups, so March is a fully post-change cohort.
flaws.correction: March is a clean post-change cohort. The 'understates the effect' argument has no basis.

flaws.location: the two most recent cohorts are retaining 68% of users, against the 41-42% we used to see
flaws.description: Compares month-1 retention of the latest cohorts with month-3 retention of the earlier cohorts, which are different horizons.
flaws.correction: Compare like with like. May/June M1 is 68% against January/February M1 of 60%/59%, and May M2 is 55% against 48%/47%. May and June contain no migrated users, so these are organic comparisons and they do suggest an early-stage improvement.

flaws.location: If the month-on-month improvement in M1 retention continues at this pace, month-1 retention should reach about 75% by the end of the year
flaws.description: Extrapolates a short, already-flattening series (May and June are both 68%) into a forecast, and assumes month-3 retention will follow.
flaws.correction: Four data points that plateau do not support a trend forecast. Report the observed values only.

open_extensions: Organic-only comparison at M1 and M2 shows a real early-stage effect may exist: organic March and April M1 is 60.0% and 62.9% (vs 60%/59% before) and May/June M1 is 68%, so the onboarding flow may lift early retention without (yet) moving M3. When May and June mature to M3, they will be the decisive cohorts.

Report the conditional retention curve (M2/M1 and M3/M2) for organic users. Organic March M3/M1 is 708/1,080 = 65.6% vs January 840/1,200 = 70.0%, which suggests any early gain may be partly offset by later churn.
Put an uncertainty interval on the cohort differences (e.g. a two-proportion CI on pooled pre vs post organic M3), since month-to-month variation of about 1 point is visible in the pre-period.

question: What is the own-price elasticity of demand for the chain's large latte, what did the September price rise do to weekly latte revenue, and should the price be raised again to £4.00?
data:
Six-store coffee chain. On 1 September the price of a large latte rose from £3.20 to £3.60. No other prices changed. Compare the 4 weeks of August (baseline) with the 8 weeks of September-October. Use simple percentage changes from the August baseline (not midpoint/arc formulas).

| Product | Aug: avg units per week | Sep-Oct: avg units per week | Price |
| Large latte, all 6 stores | 9,000 | 8,100 | £3.20 then £3.60 |
| Medium latte, all 6 stores | 7,000 | 7,700 | £2.90 throughout |

Operations log: Store 4, which normally sells about 1,500 large lattes and about 1,150 medium lattes a week, was closed for refurbishment for 2 of the 8 weeks in October. Its zero-sales weeks are included in the Sep-Oct averages above. All other stores traded normally throughout.

Ingredient and serving costs are about the same for both sizes, so finance will judge the change mainly on revenue across both latte sizes. No price above £3.60 has ever been charged at any store.
draft:
**Large latte price rise: elasticity and revenue**

**What changed.** On 1 September the large latte went from £3.20 to £3.60, a price rise of 11.1% (£0.40 on £3.60). Nothing else on the menu changed, which gives us a clean before-and-after comparison: four weeks of August against eight weeks of September and October.

**Volume response.** Large latte sales fell from 9,000 to 8,100 a week, a 10% drop. Dividing the change in quantity by the change in price gives an own-price elasticity of about −0.90 (−10% / 11.1%). An elasticity between 0 and −1 means demand is inelastic: customers cut back by proportionally less than the price went up, so revenue from the product rises.

**Revenue.** That is exactly what happened. Weekly large-latte revenue moved from £28,800 (9,000 × £3.20) to £29,160 (8,100 × £3.60), an increase of £360 a week or 1.25%. Over a year that is worth roughly £18,700 to the chain, before any change in costs, which finance tells us are essentially unaffected by the mix of sizes.

**Substitution.** A common worry with a price rise on one size is that customers simply trade down to a smaller, cheaper option, which would mean the 'lost' large lattes are not really lost but cannibalised at a lower price. We checked this. Medium latte sales were essentially flat at around 7,000 a week, so there is no sign of customers trading down to the cheaper size. The lost large-latte volume therefore reflects customers who bought less often or went elsewhere, and the revenue gain above is the whole story.

**Should we go to £4.00?** A further rise from £3.60 to £4.00 is another £0.40. Since demand is inelastic, a further rise to £4.00 should raise revenue again by a similar amount, adding perhaps another £350-£400 a week. The case looks attractive, given that revenue rose after the first increase.

**Caveats.** Eight weeks is a reasonable but not long window, and September is a month when regular customers return from holidays, so there may be some seasonality in the comparison. The elasticity estimate also relies on all six stores trading normally across both periods. We have not used a control group, because all stores took the price rise at the same time. We also have only four weeks of baseline data, so ordinary week-to-week variation in sales could move the estimate somewhat; a longer baseline would help in future.

**Recommendation.** Treat the September rise as a success. Plan a second rise to £4.00 in the new year, and review the numbers after another eight weeks.

flaws.location: a price rise of 11.1% (£0.40 on £3.60)
flaws.description: The percentage change is computed on the new price instead of the August baseline the brief specifies.
flaws.correction: £0.40 / £3.20 = 12.5%. The elasticity on the draft's own volume figure is −10% / 12.5% = −0.80, not −0.90.

flaws.location: Large latte sales fell from 9,000 to 8,100 a week, a 10% drop
flaws.description: Ignores Store 4's two-week closure, which removed about 3,000 large lattes (375 a week on average) from the Sep-Oct figure. The draft's caveat even assumes all stores traded normally.
flaws.correction: Closure-adjusted Sep-Oct volume is about 8,100 + 375 = 8,475 a week, a 5.8% fall. Elasticity is about −0.47 and large-latte revenue is about £30,510 a week (+5.9%), not +1.25%.

flaws.location: Medium latte sales were essentially flat at around 7,000 a week, so there is no sign of customers trading down to the cheaper size
flaws.description: The data shows medium latte sales rose from 7,000 to 7,700 a week (+10%), or about 7,990 (+14%) after adjusting for Store 4. This is clear evidence of trading down.
flaws.correction: Medium-latte revenue rose from £20,300 to £22,330 a week (about £23,160 adjusted). Total latte revenue rose from £49,100 to £51,490 (raw), and part of the 'lost' large volume moved to medium.

flaws.location: Since demand is inelastic, a further rise to £4.00 should raise revenue again by a similar amount
flaws.description: Extrapolates a single local elasticity estimate to a price never charged. Elasticity typically rises as price increases, and the substitution to medium makes the response larger than the large-latte figure suggests.
flaws.correction: The data cannot predict the response at £4.00. A trial at a subset of stores, with comparison stores, would be needed.

open_extensions: Compute a cross-price elasticity of medium lattes with respect to the large-latte price: roughly +10% / 12.5% = +0.8 raw, or about +1.1 closure-adjusted. This quantifies cannibalisation and shows the combined latte category is what matters.
Repeat the analysis excluding Store 4 entirely (five stores, both periods) as a cleaner robustness check than imputing its missing weeks; this requires store-level weekly data.
Use the arc (midpoint) elasticity as a sensitivity check, since the price change is large: on the adjusted volumes (−6.0% / 11.8%) it is about −0.51, close to the simple-percentage estimate.

question: How many agents should be rostered for the Monday 09:00-10:00 interval, and how does that compare with the 48 currently rostered?
data:
Inbound customer-service team, planning the Monday 09:00-10:00 interval.

- Forecast calls offered, Monday 09:00-10:00: 360. This forecast is already specific to Monday mornings: it was built from the last 8 Mondays and includes the usual Monday uplift of about 15% over other weekdays.
- Average talk time: 300 seconds per call.
- Average after-call work (wrap-up notes and logging): 45 seconds per call. Agents cannot take a new call during wrap-up.
- Average handle time (AHT) = talk time + after-call work.
- Workload in agent-hours = calls × AHT (seconds) / 3,600.
- Target occupancy: 85% (share of logged-in time agents spend handling calls). Productive agents needed = workload / occupancy.
- Shrinkage: 30% of rostered time is lost to breaks, training, coaching and absence. Planning convention: rostered agents = productive agents / (1 − shrinkage).
- Round the final rostered figure up to a whole agent.
- Currently rostered for this interval: 48 agents.
- Service-level history: on the last 8 Mondays, 09:00-10:00 averaged 61% of calls answered within 20 seconds against an 80% target, and an abandonment rate of 9%.
draft:
**Monday 09:00-10:00 staffing requirement**

**Purpose.** This note sets out how many agents we need to roster for the Monday morning peak hour, using our standard workload method, and compares that with the current roster of 48. The interval has averaged well below its service-level target over the last 8 Mondays.

**Step 1: Call volume.** The planning forecast for 09:00-10:00 is 360 calls. However, the 360 forecast is a weekday average, so I have applied the standard 15% Monday uplift, giving 414 calls for the Monday interval. Monday volumes run above other weekdays, and planning on an average day would leave us exposed.

**Step 2: Handle time.** Average handle time is 300 seconds (5 minutes) per call. I have not added any buffer for variation.

**Step 3: Workload.** Workload is the total time agents must spend handling calls in the interval, i.e. calls multiplied by handle time: 414 × 5 minutes = 2,070 minutes, or 34.5 agent-hours of call handling that must be delivered within the hour.

**Step 4: Occupancy.** We do not want agents occupied 100% of the time, because that leads to fatigue, burnout and long queues. At our 85% occupancy target, the number of productive agents needed is 34.5 ÷ 0.85 = 39.6 productive agents.

**Step 5: Shrinkage.** Not everyone rostered is actually available to take calls: breaks, training, coaching and absence take 30% of rostered time. Allowing for this, 39.6 × 1.30 = 51.5 rostered agents, which rounds up to 52.

**Comparison with the current roster.** We currently roster 48 agents for this interval, so we are short by 4 agents. This is consistent with the service-level history: over the last 8 Mondays only 61% of calls were answered within 20 seconds, against an 80% target, and 9% of callers abandoned. A shortfall of about 8% of the required roster would plausibly produce a miss of this size.

**Options.**
1. Move 4 agents' start times from 10:00 to 09:00 on Mondays. This is cost-neutral but will thin out the 10:00-11:00 interval, which would need checking.
2. Schedule no training or coaching sessions in the first hour on Mondays. This reduces shrinkage for this interval and could recover some capacity.
3. Add 4 part-time agents on a Monday-morning shift pattern.

**Recommendation.** Roster 52 agents for Monday 09:00-10:00, starting with option 2 (no training in the first hour) and topping up with option 1. Re-run the calculation each quarter as the forecast is refreshed. If option 2 is adopted, the shrinkage figure for this interval should be re-estimated before the next planning round.

flaws.location: the 360 forecast is a weekday average, so I have applied the standard 15% Monday uplift
flaws.description: The data states the 360 forecast is already Monday-specific and already includes the Monday uplift. Applying 15% again double-counts it.
flaws.correction: Use 360 calls, not 414.

flaws.location: Average handle time is 300 seconds (5 minutes) per call
flaws.description: Uses talk time only. The data gives 45 seconds of after-call work per call, during which agents cannot take calls, and defines AHT as talk + wrap.
flaws.correction: AHT = 345 seconds. With 360 calls, workload = 360 × 345 / 3,600 = 34.5 agent-hours. (The draft's 34.5 is right only by coincidence: two errors offset.)

flaws.location: 34.5 ÷ 0.85 = 39.6 productive agents
flaws.description: Arithmetic error: 34.5 / 0.85 = 40.6.
flaws.correction: 40.6 productive agents.

flaws.location: 39.6 × 1.30 = 51.5 rostered agents
flaws.description: Applies shrinkage by multiplying by (1 + 0.30) instead of dividing by (1 − 0.30), as the planning convention requires. This understates the roster.
flaws.correction: 40.6 / 0.70 = 58.0, so 58 rostered agents (10 more than the current 48, not 4).

open_extensions: Workload-based staffing ignores queueing. An Erlang C check at 34.5 Erlangs (360 calls, 345 s AHT) shows 40 logged-in agents give about 80% answered within 20 s (39 give about 73%). This agrees with the 40.6 from the occupancy method and supports roughly 58 rostered.

Sensitivity analysis: each 10% error in the call forecast moves the requirement by about 6 rostered agents (58 × 0.1), and each 5-point change in shrinkage moves it by about 4-5. Interval-level shrinkage for Monday 09:00 (e.g. with training barred) may differ from the 30% average.
Use the 9% abandonment to sanity-check demand: handled calls understate offered demand, and repeat calls from abandoners may already be inflating the 360 forecast.

question: What does this year's engagement survey say about overall employee satisfaction, how has it changed since last year, and which department needs attention?
data:
Annual employee engagement survey, three departments, 1,200 employees in total. Key item: 'Overall, I am satisfied working here' (agree = 'satisfied').

Last year: 600 of 1,150 employees responded, and 62% of respondents were satisfied.

This year:
| Department | Headcount | Responses | Satisfied |
| Engineering | 300 | 180 | 126 |
| Sales | 400 | 120 | 60 |
| Operations | 500 | 240 | 132 |
| Total | 1,200 | 540 | 318 |

The survey contained no questions about pay, commission, shift patterns or line management, and free-text comments were not coded this year.

Context from HR: Sales moved to a new commission scheme in January. Operations introduced a new shift pattern in March. Engineering had no structural changes. The survey was anonymous and open for two weeks in May; Sales staff were at the annual sales conference for four of those ten working days.
draft:
**Engagement survey: results and priorities**

**Response.** This year 540 of 1,200 employees responded, a 47% response rate. That is lower than we would like but is enough to give a reliable picture at company level.

**Overall satisfaction.** Of the 540 respondents, 318 said they were satisfied working here, which is 58.9%. This is down from 65% last year, a fall of six points. A drop of that size in a single year is a clear signal that engagement is weakening across the company, and the board should treat it as a priority.

**By department.**
- Engineering: 126 of 180 respondents satisfied (70%).
- Sales: 60 of 120 satisfied (50%).
- Operations: 132 of 240 satisfied (55%).

Engineering is comfortably the most positive department. Operations has the largest number of satisfied staff (132), making it the healthiest department by this measure, with a broad base of positive employees. Sales is the clear outlier at the bottom, with only half of respondents satisfied.

**Why is Sales low?** The low score in Sales is clearly a reaction to the new commission scheme introduced in January. Sales staff had a significant change to how they are paid early in the year, and dissatisfaction with pay is a well-known driver of disengagement. We would expect satisfaction to recover once the scheme has bedded in, or sooner if the scheme is adjusted.

**Response rates.** Response rates differed between departments: 60% in Engineering, 30% in Sales and 48% in Operations. The Sales figure is particularly low, partly because the survey window overlapped with the sales conference. We should bear this in mind, but the Sales result is still based on 120 people, which is a reasonable sample.

**Priorities.**
1. Sales: review the commission scheme with the Sales leadership team and run listening sessions to understand the specific concerns.
2. Company-wide: the six-point fall needs a response. We suggest a short pulse survey in the autumn to track whether satisfaction is still falling.
3. Operations: as the healthiest department, Operations could share practices with Sales, for example around team communication.

**Next year.** We recommend adding questions on pay, workload and management so that we can diagnose causes directly, coding free-text comments, and avoiding clashes with major events so that response rates are more even.

**Reporting.** Results should be shared with each department head alongside their department's response rate, so that small or unrepresentative samples are visible when the results are discussed. We also suggest publishing the company-level result to all staff with a short summary of the agreed actions.

flaws.correction: Response rate 45.0%.

flaws.location: This is down from 65% last year, a fall of six points
flaws.description: The data gives last year's satisfaction as 62%, not 65%.
flaws.correction: The fall is 62% to 58.9%, i.e. 3.1 points. With about 600 and 540 respondents this is within sampling noise (z of about 1.1), so 'a clear signal' is not supported.

flaws.location: Operations has the largest number of satisfied staff (132), making it the healthiest department
flaws.description: Ranks departments on counts of satisfied respondents, which reflect department size and response numbers, rather than on rates.
flaws.correction: By rate, Operations is 55%, below Engineering (70%) and only 5 points above Sales (50%). Engineering is the healthiest; Operations is not a model for Sales.

flaws.location: The low score in Sales is clearly a reaction to the new commission scheme introduced in January
flaws.description: Asserts a cause the survey cannot test (no pay or commission questions, no prior-year department breakdown). Operations also had a structural change and also scores low.
flaws.correction: The data shows Sales scores lowest, not why. Last year's Sales figure and targeted questions would be needed to attribute it to commission.

open_extensions: Weight to headcount to correct for unequal response rates: (0.70×300 + 0.50×400 + 0.55×500) / 1,200 = 57.1%, slightly below the raw 58.9%, because the most positive department is over-represented among respondents.
Report confidence intervals by department. Sales at 60/120 has a 95% CI of roughly ±9 points, so Sales vs Operations (55%) is not clearly different, while Engineering is clearly higher than both.

Non-response sensitivity for Sales: with only 30% responding (partly due to the conference), show the range of plausible department satisfaction if non-respondents were 10 points more or less satisfied than respondents.

question: Which food item at the wedding reception was the most likely vehicle of the gastrointestinal outbreak, and what does the evidence say about wider risk from the caterer?
data:
Gastrointestinal illness after a wedding reception (Saturday evening buffet). All 120 guests who ate at the reception were interviewed. 48 met the case definition: diarrhoea and/or vomiting with onset 12-72 hours after the meal.

Food-specific exposure:
| Food | Ate: total | Ate: ill | Did not eat: total | Did not eat: ill |
| Chicken skewers | 80 | 40 | 40 | 8 |
| Prawn salad | 50 | 35 | 70 | 13 |
| Rice | 100 | 42 | 20 | 6 |
| Chocolate mousse | 60 | 30 | 60 | 18 |

Notes from the environmental health officer:
- The caterer cooked one batch of rice on Saturday morning. Part of it was served at the wedding; the rest went to a 90-person corporate lunch the same day. All 90 lunch attendees were contacted and none reported illness.
- The prawns were bought ready-defrosted, and the prawn salad was assembled about 6 hours before service and held at room temperature.
- The caterer supplied four other events that week, using different menus. No illness reports have been received from them so far, though not all attendees have been contacted.
- Stool samples are awaited.
draft:
**Wedding reception outbreak: preliminary analysis**

**Overview.** Of 120 guests who ate at the reception, 48 met the case definition, an overall attack rate of 40%. All guests were interviewed, so there is no non-response bias in the food histories.

**Food-specific attack rates.**
- Chicken skewers: 50% among those who ate them (40/80) versus 20% among those who did not (8/40), a relative risk of 2.5.
- Prawn salad: 70% among those who ate it versus 13% among those who did not, a relative risk of about 5.4.
- Rice: 42% among eaters (42/100) versus 30% among non-eaters (6/20), a relative risk of 1.4.
- Chocolate mousse: 50% (30/60) versus 30% (18/60), a relative risk of about 1.7.

Every item has a relative risk above 1, which is typical when several dishes are eaten together and illness is common.

**Which food best explains the outbreak?** A useful test of a candidate vehicle is how many of the cases it can account for. Here rice stands out: 42 of the 48 cases (88%) ate rice, more than for any other dish, so rice is the most likely vehicle. By contrast only 35 cases ate prawn salad, leaving 13 cases unexplained, and 40 ate chicken, leaving 8. Although prawn salad has the highest attack rate, a vehicle that misses more than a quarter of the cases is a weaker candidate. Rice was also the dish most guests ate, and bulk-cooked rice held warm is a common source of food poisoning, so it is a plausible vehicle.

**Onset.** All cases had onset 12-72 hours after the meal, but this is built into the case definition, so it cannot by itself distinguish a single exposure from later spread. Individual onset times are being collected to build an epidemic curve.

**Wider risk.** The caterer served four other events this week. Because the wedding meal produced an attack rate of 40%, it is reasonable to estimate that about 40% of people who ate food from this caterer this week will have been ill, and the public health team should plan its follow-up on that basis.

**Recommended actions.**
1. Treat rice as the probable vehicle and review the caterer's rice cooking, cooling and reheating practices.
2. Contact attendees of the caterer's other events this week, prioritising the largest.
3. Await stool sample results to confirm the organism.
4. Advise the caterer to suspend bulk rice service until the review is complete.

**Limitations.** Food histories rely on recall, and some guests may have misremembered what they ate, especially at a buffet. Small numbers in some cells (for example the 20 guests who did not eat rice) make some relative risks imprecise.

flaws.location: 70% among those who ate it versus 13% among those who did not
flaws.description: 13 is the number of ill non-eaters, not the percentage: 13 / 70 = 18.6%.
flaws.correction: Attack rate in non-eaters 18.6%; relative risk 70% / 18.6% = 3.8, still the highest of any food.

flaws.location: 42 of the 48 cases (88%) ate rice, more than for any other dish, so rice is the most likely vehicle
flaws.description: Uses the share of cases exposed rather than attack rates or relative risk. Rice was eaten by 100 of 120 guests, so most cases would have eaten it whatever the vehicle.
flaws.correction: Compare attack rates and RRs: prawn salad has the highest RR (3.8) and the largest attack-rate difference (70% vs 18.6%). Rice (RR 1.4) is the weakest association.

flaws.location: Rice was also the dish most guests ate, and bulk-cooked rice held warm is a common source of food poisoning, so it is a plausible vehicle
flaws.description: Ignores that the same rice batch was served to 90 people at a corporate lunch with no illness. It also ignores the prawn salad's documented 6 hours at room temperature.
flaws.correction: The rice is effectively exonerated. The handling evidence supports prawn salad as the vehicle.

flaws.location: it is reasonable to estimate that about 40% of people who ate food from this caterer this week will have been ill
flaws.description: Generalises the wedding attack rate to other events with different menus, for which there are no cases so far.
flaws.correction: The wedding data say nothing about risk at other events. The risk depends on whether the vehicle (likely prawn salad) was served there. Follow-up should target events that served prawns or used the same preparation.

open_extensions: Cross-tabulate prawn salad against chicken (2×2×2) to check whether the chicken association (RR 2.5) is confounded by guests who ate both, e.g. through a stratified RR or Mantel-Haenszel estimate.

Note that 13 cases did not eat prawn salad. Explore misclassification of exposure (recall at a buffet), cross-contamination of other dishes, or secondary cases. Then, once onset times are available, check whether these 13 cases have later onsets.

Compute the population attributable fraction for prawn salad: (overall AR − AR in unexposed) / overall AR = (40% − 18.6%) / 40%, about 54%, which quantifies how much of the outbreak the vehicle accounts for.

question: How much did the Year 8 small-group maths tutoring programme improve tutored students' test scores, and would making it compulsory for the whole year group raise average attainment?
data:
Year 8 maths tutoring programme, one school, 2024-25.

In September, teachers nominated 75 students they considered to be struggling in maths. These students were offered small-group tutoring (two sessions a week, September to May). The other 140 Year 8 students were not tutored. All students sit the same standardised maths test (scored 0-100) in autumn and in summer.

| Group | Students with both tests | Autumn mean | Summer mean |
| Tutored | 60 | 42 | 54 |
| Not tutored | 140 | 58 | 63 |

15 of the 75 nominated students left the programme before summer (moved school, stopped attending, or were withdrawn by parents). They are excluded from the table above. Their autumn mean was 35. 11 of the 15 were still at the school and sat the summer test; their summer mean was 38.

Test publisher's note: the autumn-to-summer test-retest correlation is about 0.7. Students selected because of low scores on one sitting typically score closer to the average on the next sitting, even without any intervention.

The school is considering making tutoring compulsory for all 215 Year 8 students next year.
draft:
**Year 8 maths tutoring: impact evaluation**

**Background.** In September, 75 Year 8 students judged to be struggling in maths were offered twice-weekly small-group tutoring. This note estimates the programme's effect on standardised test scores and advises on the proposal to extend tutoring to the whole year group. Tutoring ran from September to May, and all students sat the same standardised paper in autumn and summer, so scores are directly comparable across the year.

**Design.** Students were randomly allocated to tutoring, so the tutored and untutored groups should be comparable apart from the tutoring itself, and differences in progress can be attributed to the programme. The analysis is based on the 60 tutored and 140 untutored students with both test scores. Both groups took the same standardised test in autumn and summer, scored 0-100.

**Results.**
- Tutored students: autumn mean 42, summer mean 54.
- Untutored students: autumn mean 58, summer mean 63.

The tutored group started well behind (16 points below the untutored group in autumn) and closed much of that gap by summer, finishing 9 points behind. The gap narrowed by 7 points over the year.

**Estimating the effect.** The untutored group also improved, from 58 to 63, which reflects normal progress under ordinary classroom teaching. Because the untutored group's improvement reflects ordinary teaching rather than anything the programme did, the fairest measure of the programme is the tutored group's own progress. The tutored group's mean rose by 12 points, from 42 to 54, so the programme added 12 points to tutored students' scores. That is a large effect for a single year.

**Consistency.** The gain was achieved with a relatively light-touch model (two sessions a week in small groups), which makes it cheaper to scale than one-to-one tutoring.

**Extending the programme.** The proposal is to make tutoring compulsory for all 215 Year 8 students next year. Making tutoring compulsory for all 215 Year 8 students should therefore raise the year-group average by about 12 points. Even if the effect for stronger students were somewhat smaller, the programme would still lift the year-group average substantially.

**Costs and practicalities.** Extending to 215 students would roughly triple the number of groups needed. Timetabling would need to change, and we would need to recruit or redeploy tutors. These costs should be set against the size of the expected gain.

**Recommendation.** The evaluation shows a strong positive effect of tutoring. We recommend extending it to all Year 8 students next year and continuing to monitor results with the same autumn and summer tests.

flaws.location: Students were randomly allocated to tutoring
flaws.description: The data says students were nominated by teachers because they were struggling, not randomly allocated. Selection on low scores also brings regression to the mean (the publisher's note).
flaws.correction: This is a non-randomised comparison of a low-scoring selected group with everyone else. Group differences cannot be attributed cleanly to the programme, and part of the tutored gain is expected regression to the mean.

flaws.location: The tutored group's mean rose by 12 points, from 42 to 54, so the programme added 12 points
flaws.description: Uses the raw pre-post gain and ignores the comparison group's gain of 5 points, i.e. ignores the baseline improvement everyone made.
flaws.correction: Difference-in-differences: 12 − 5 = 7 points (the draft itself notes the gap narrowed by 7). Even this is an upper bound, given regression to the mean.

flaws.location: The analysis is based on the 60 tutored and 140 untutored students with both test scores
flaws.description: Ignores the 15 nominated students who left the programme. They started lower (autumn mean 35), and the 11 who were tested gained only 3 points. Excluding them inflates the tutored group's gain.
flaws.correction: Including the 11 tested leavers (intention to treat): autumn mean 2,905/71 = 40.9, summer 3,658/71 = 51.5, gain 10.6. DiD 10.6 − 5 = about 5.6 points, before any allowance for regression to the mean.

flaws.location: Making tutoring compulsory for all 215 Year 8 students should therefore raise the year-group average by about 12 points
flaws.description: Generalises an effect estimated on teacher-nominated low-attaining students to the whole year group, including higher attainers, and to a compulsory programme.
flaws.correction: The data cannot support any estimate for students who were not struggling or for a compulsory programme. At most, a modest effect on nominated low attainers is suggested.

open_extensions: Estimate the regression-to-the-mean component. With a test-retest correlation of 0.7 and a cohort mean of about 53 in autumn ((60×42 + 140×58)/200 = 53.2), a group 11 points below the mean would be expected to move about 0.3 × 11, or roughly 3 points, towards it without any intervention. This shrinks the DiD estimate further.
Propose a stronger design for next year: randomise tutoring among nominated students (or use a waiting list), which would let the school estimate the effect without selection bias.
Report the distribution, not just means: e.g. the proportion of tutored students moving above a pass threshold, and whether gains were concentrated among a few students.

question: Which supplier, A or B, should the firm use for component K-220, given that a delivery taking longer than 26 days causes a stockout?
data:
Choosing a supplier for component K-220. Safety stock covers lead times of up to 26 days. Any delivery that takes longer than 26 days causes a stockout, which halts the assembly line.

Last 12 orders from each supplier, lead time in days (order placed to goods received), in date order:
Supplier A (sea freight): 21, 23, 22, 24, 20, 22, 45, 23, 21, 22, 24, 21
Supplier B (road and rail): 18, 19, 30, 17, 29, 18, 31, 19, 28, 18, 30, 19

Notes:
- A's 45-day delivery was the order shipped in February, during the documented three-week national port strike, which delayed all sea freight that month. There has been no strike since, and none is planned.
- B had no comparable disruption. B's deliveries of 28 days or more are spread throughout the year.
- Unit price: A £4.10, B £4.05. Annual volume about 40,000 units.
- Both suppliers meet the quality specification for K-220.
- This decision applies to K-220 only. Other components are bought under separate contracts with different specifications, volumes and routes.
draft:
**Supplier choice for K-220: lead-time analysis**

**Objective.** Recommend a supplier for K-220 based on delivery performance over the last 12 orders from each, with price as a secondary factor. Our safety stock covers lead times of up to 26 days. A stockout halts the assembly line, so reliability of delivery matters more than small differences in price.

**Data.** The analysis covers the last 12 orders from each supplier, measured from order placement to goods received. Supplier A ships by sea; Supplier B uses road and rail.

**Average lead time.** Supplier A averages 24.0 days across its 12 orders. Supplier B averages 22.0 days, two days quicker. B's typical delivery is also quick: half of its orders arrived in 19 days or fewer, compared with 22 days or fewer for A. Both averages sit within the 26-day cover.

**Spread.** A's lead times range from 20 to 45 days and B's from 17 to 31 days, a spread of 25 days for A and 14 for B. A had one very long delivery of 45 days, which pulls its average up and shows the kind of risk that comes with sea freight: a single disruption can push a delivery far beyond our safety-stock cover. B's worst case, 31 days, is much less extreme.

**Decision rule.** Since B delivers faster on average and its worst delivery is 14 days shorter than A's worst, B is the better choice against our 26-day safety-stock cover. Lower average lead time means stock arrives sooner and our cover is used less.

**Price.** B is also slightly cheaper: £4.05 per unit against £4.10. On about 40,000 units a year, that saves £2,000 annually. Price is not the main driver here, but it reinforces the lead-time case. The difference is 5p per unit, about 1% of the unit price.

**Quality.** Both suppliers meet the K-220 quality specification, so quality does not discriminate between them.

**Wider implications.** Since B is the more efficient supplier, we should also move our other components to B when their contracts come up for renewal, consolidating volume with one dependable partner and strengthening our negotiating position.

**Recommendation.** Award the K-220 contract to Supplier B. Review lead-time performance quarterly, and keep A as a qualified back-up supplier in case B's performance deteriorates. Switching will require a new supply agreement and a first trial order to confirm packaging and labelling before volumes move across. We suggest placing the first two orders with B alongside a final order from A, so that any teething problems do not leave the line short.

flaws.location: Supplier B averages 22.0 days, two days quicker
flaws.description: B's 12 lead times sum to 276, so the mean is 23.0 days, not 22.0.
flaws.correction: B mean 23.0 days, one day quicker than A's 24.0 (A sums to 288).

flaws.location: A had one very long delivery of 45 days, which pulls its average up and shows the kind of risk that comes with sea freight
flaws.description: Ignores that the 45-day delivery was caused by a documented one-off national port strike that delayed all sea freight.
flaws.correction: Excluding the strike order, A's other 11 deliveries average 243/11 = 22.1 days (below B's 23.0), with a maximum of 24 days and no deliveries over 26.

flaws.location: Since B delivers faster on average and its worst delivery is 14 days shorter than A's worst, B is the better choice against our 26-day safety-stock cover
flaws.description: The stockout criterion depends on how often lead time exceeds 26 days, not on the mean or the single worst case.
flaws.correction: Exceedances over 26 days: A 1 of 12 (8%, the strike order), B 5 of 12 (42%: 30, 29, 31, 28, 30). B caused a stockout on 5 of its last 12 orders. Choose A.

flaws.location: Since B is the more efficient supplier, we should also move our other components to B when their contracts come up for renewal
flaws.description: Generalises from one component's lead-time record to other components with different specifications, routes and contracts. It also rests on the flawed conclusion that B is better.
flaws.correction: The data say nothing about B's performance on other components. No recommendation beyond K-220 is supported.

open_extensions: Quantify the cost trade-off: B saves £2,000 a year on price, against stockouts on about 5 in every 12 orders, each of which halts the line. Even a modest cost per stockout outweighs the saving.

Note that B's lead times look bimodal (17-19 days or 28-31 days). Ask B what drives the slow orders (e.g. consolidation or rail scheduling); if the cause is controllable, B could become viable, perhaps with a longer order cycle.

Model safety stock directly: to cover B's observed maximum of 31 days, cover would need to rise by 5 days (about 550 units at 40,000 a year), with holding cost that can be set against the price difference.

question: Did guard X's three-point shooting genuinely improve after the mid-season change of shooting coach, and should X take a larger share of the team's three-point attempts next season?
data:
Professional basketball. Guard X's shooting before and after a mid-season change of shooting coach, which took effect after game 30. X played in all 50 games. His minutes per game were similar in both periods (about 32).

Shooting percentage = makes / attempts.

| | Games 1-30 | Games 31-50 |
| Three-point attempts | 150 | 80 |
| Three-point makes | 51 | 32 |
| Free-throw attempts | 100 | 70 |
| Free-throw makes | 80 | 55 |

League average three-point percentage this season: 36%.

Opponent breakdown: in games 31-50, 30 of X's 80 three-point attempts came in 4 games against the league's two worst-ranked perimeter defences, and he made 18 of those 30. X did not face either of those teams in games 1-30.

The coaching staff must decide whether to increase X's share of team three-point attempts next season. The new shooting coach worked with the whole squad, not just X.
draft:
**Guard X: three-point shooting since the coaching change**

**Summary.** X has become a markedly better three-point shooter since the change of shooting coach after game 30, and the data support giving him more of the team's three-point attempts next season.

**Data.** Figures are X's totals for the season, split at game 30.

**Context.** The new shooting coach took over after game 30 and works with the whole squad. X played in all 50 games, so neither period is affected by injury absences.

**Before and after.** In games 1-30, X made 51 of 150 three-point attempts, 34.0%, a little below the league average of 36%. On 80 attempts since the change he has made 32, a 40.0% rate, comfortably above the league average. That is an improvement of 6 percentage points, a relative improvement of 21%. Over a typical season of attempts, a 6-point gain in percentage is worth a substantial number of extra points.

**Volume.** X attempted 5.0 threes per game before the change (150 in 30 games) and 4.0 per game afterwards (80 in 20 games). In total he took 230 threes across the 50 games. He is taking slightly fewer threes per game but converting a higher share of them.

**Supporting evidence.** His free-throw percentage also rose, from 80% to 86%, over the same period. Free throws are a pure measure of shooting technique, unaffected by defence or shot selection, so an improvement there is good corroboration that the coaching has changed his mechanics rather than the result being a lucky streak.

**Interpretation.** The new coach has turned X into a 40% three-point shooter, and he should take a larger share of the team's threes next season. At 40%, a three-point attempt is worth 1.2 points on average, compared with 1.02 at his old rate of 34% and 1.08 at the league average, so shifting attempts towards X adds expected points with no extra possessions.

**Caveats.** Twenty games is a shorter window than thirty, and shooting percentages fluctuate. The new rate should therefore be monitored as more games are played. Shooting is also affected by role, shot difficulty and team-mates' passing, none of which is captured in these totals.

**Recommendation.** Increase X's share of team three-point attempts next season, design more catch-and-shoot sets for him, and continue his individual work with the new shooting coach. Opponents will adjust their defensive plans if X's role grows, so the staff should review his efficiency after the first 20 games of next season and scale his share back if his rate falls.

flaws.location: a relative improvement of 21%
flaws.description: A 6-point rise from 34% is 6/34 = 17.6% in relative terms, not 21%.
flaws.correction: Relative improvement of about 18%.

flaws.location: On 80 attempts since the change he has made 32, a 40.0% rate
flaws.description: Ignores that 30 of the 80 post-change attempts (18 made) came against the two worst perimeter defences, which X did not face before the change.
flaws.correction: Against other opponents after the change X made 14 of 50 (28%), below his pre-change 34%. The apparent improvement is driven by schedule.

flaws.location: His free-throw percentage also rose, from 80% to 86%
flaws.description: The data show free throws went from 80/100 = 80% to 55/70 = 78.6%, a slight fall.
flaws.correction: Free-throw shooting did not improve, so it provides no corroboration of better mechanics.

flaws.location: The new coach has turned X into a 40% three-point shooter
flaws.description: Draws a causal, stable conclusion from 80 attempts. The pre/post difference is not statistically significant (two-proportion z of about 0.9), it is confounded by opponent quality, and the coach changed for the whole squad.
flaws.correction: The evidence is consistent with no change in X's true shooting ability. No reallocation of attempts is justified on these data.

open_extensions: Give interval estimates: 32/80 has a 95% CI of roughly 29-51%, and 51/150 of roughly 26-42%. The intervals overlap heavily, which shows how little 20 games can establish.

Use the whole squad as a comparison. Since the coach worked with everyone, compare teammates' pre/post three-point percentages (ideally against the same opponents) to separate a coaching effect from schedule effects.
Apply regression to the league mean (e.g. empirical-Bayes shrinkage towards 36% based on attempts) to estimate X's likely true rate before setting next season's shot allocation.

question: Under the council's affordability rule, can a median-income household in the city afford to buy the median house, or to rent a median 2-bedroom flat?
data:
City housing affordability, 2025.

- Median house price: £320,000. Lower-quartile house price: £230,000.
- Median gross household income: £40,000 a year. Median take-home (net) household income: £2,700 a month.
- Over the past year, median house prices rose 6% and median household incomes rose 3%.
- First-time-buyer assumptions: 10% deposit, 25-year capital-repayment mortgage at 5.0% fixed interest.
  - Monthly repayment on a £288,000 loan (median house): £1,684.
  - Monthly repayment on a £207,000 loan (lower-quartile house): £1,210.
- Median rent, 2-bedroom flat: £1,150 a month.
- Council affordability rule: housing costs are 'affordable' if they take no more than 35% of net (take-home) household income.
- Repayment figures use the standard repayment-mortgage formula and exclude insurance and maintenance. Rents exclude bills.
- Income figures cover all household types in the city.
- The council applies the 35% rule to both renting and buying.
- No data are available on planning permissions, housing supply, or who is buying homes in the city.
draft:
**Is the city affordable for a median household?**

**Scope.** This note applies the council's affordability rule to a household on the median income, using the figures supplied. Repayments and rents exclude insurance, maintenance and bills, so real housing costs are somewhat higher than the figures below.

**Price-to-income ratio.** The median house costs £320,000 and median gross household income is £40,000, a ratio of 8.0. A common rule of thumb treats ratios above about 5 as seriously unaffordable, so on this measure the city is well beyond what a typical household can stretch to.

**Buying.** A first-time buyer with a 10% deposit (£32,000) would need a £288,000 mortgage. Over 25 years at 5.0%, the monthly repayment is £1,684, and total repayments would come to just over £505,000. That £1,684 is 52% of the median take-home pay of £2,700, well above the council's 35% threshold. Buying the median home is therefore unaffordable for a median household, before even considering how long it would take to save the £32,000 deposit.

Even the lower-quartile house, at £230,000, needs a £207,000 loan and a monthly repayment of £1,210, which is 45% of take-home pay. So for a median household, even the cheaper end of the market fails the test.

**Renting.** The median 2-bedroom rent is £1,150 a month. Against monthly household income of £3,333 (£40,000 / 12), rent of £1,150 takes 34.5% of income, just inside the 35% threshold. Renting is therefore affordable for a median household, albeit only just, and it is the realistic tenure for most median earners in the city, although it offers no route to building equity.

**Trend.** Over the past year incomes have kept pace with prices, both rising about 6%, so the price-to-income ratio has been stable. The affordability problem is long-standing rather than getting worse, which suggests it is structural.

**Why are prices so high?** Since prices have reached eight times incomes, it is clear that planning restrictions are the main reason prices have outpaced incomes, constraining the supply of new homes relative to demand from a growing population.

**Conclusions.**
1. Buying the median house is unaffordable for a median household; even a lower-quartile house fails the 35% test.
2. Renting a median 2-bedroom flat is just affordable.
3. Policy should focus on relaxing planning constraints to increase supply.

These figures describe a household on exactly the median income. Households with two higher earners or existing equity will be better placed, and single-earner households worse placed.

flaws.location: That £1,684 is 52% of the median take-home pay of £2,700
flaws.correction: Median-house repayment = 62% of net income.

flaws.location: Against monthly household income of £3,333 (£40,000 / 12), rent of £1,150 takes 34.5% of income
flaws.description: Applies the 35% rule to gross income, but the council rule (and the draft's own buying test) uses net take-home income.
flaws.correction: £1,150 / £2,700 = 42.6% of net income, so renting a median 2-bed is also unaffordable under the rule.

flaws.location: Over the past year incomes have kept pace with prices, both rising about 6%
flaws.description: The data say prices rose 6% and incomes only 3%.
flaws.correction: The price-to-income ratio rose by about 3% (1.06/1.03) in a year; affordability is worsening.

flaws.location: it is clear that planning restrictions are the main reason prices have outpaced incomes
flaws.description: Makes a causal claim about planning restrictions, for which the data contain no evidence. The draft also invents 'a growing population'.
flaws.correction: The data describe affordability but cannot identify its causes. Supply and planning data would be needed.

open_extensions: Compute the income needed to meet the rule: buying the median house needs net income of £1,684/0.35, about £4,811 a month; renting the median 2-bed needs about £3,286 a month. This shows how far above median a household must be.
Sensitivity to the interest rate: run the repayment at 4% and 6% to show whether any plausible rate brings median buying under 35% (it does not; even 0% interest gives £960, which is 35.6%).
Add the deposit barrier: £32,000 is 11.9 months of net median income. Even saving 10% of net income (£270 a month) would take nearly 10 years.

question: Which of the three tariffs (Fixed, Variable or Time-of-use) will give the household the lowest total energy bill over the next 12 months, and by how much?
data:
A household is choosing an energy tariff for the next 12 months (365 days). It is currently on the Variable tariff and can switch freely: none of the tariffs below has an exit fee.

Last 12 months' usage: electricity 3,100 kWh, gas 12,000 kWh. About 15% of the household's current electricity use falls in the off-peak window (dishwasher and washing machine on timers).

The household takes delivery of an electric car next week. It expects to need about 2,400 kWh a year of home charging, all of which it will schedule in the off-peak window. Gas use is not expected to change.

| Tariff | Electricity unit rate | Electricity standing charge | Gas unit rate | Gas standing charge |
| Fixed (F) | 24.5p/kWh | 55p/day | 6.2p/kWh | 30p/day |
| Variable (V) | 22.0p/kWh | 60p/day | 6.0p/kWh | 31p/day |
| Time-of-use (E) | 30.0p/kWh peak; 8.0p/kWh off-peak (00:30-05:30) | 50p/day | 6.0p/kWh | 31p/day |

Rates on V can change at the supplier's discretion with 30 days' notice; the supplier has announced no change. F and E are fixed for 12 months. Ignore VAT (rates already include it).
draft:
**Energy tariff comparison for the next 12 months**

**Approach.** I have costed each tariff for a full year (365 days) using the household's actual consumption. Based on last year's usage of 3,100 kWh of electricity and 12,000 kWh of gas, the annual cost of each tariff is set out below, including standing charges.

**Assumptions.** I have assumed the household's usage over the next year will be similar to last year's, and that rates on the variable tariff stay where they are, since the supplier has announced no change. Standing charges are payable every day regardless of usage, so they are included in full.

**Fixed (F).**
- Electricity: 3,100 × 24.5p = £734.50, plus standing charge 55p × 365 = £200.75, total £935.25.
- Gas: 12,000 × 6.2p = £744.00, plus 30p × 365 = £109.50, total £853.50.
- Total: £1,788.75. The fixed tariff also carries exit fees of £75 per fuel, so switching to F and then away again later would add £150, bringing its effective cost to £1,938.75.

**Variable (V).**
- Electricity: 3,100 × 22.0p = £682.00, plus 60p × 365 = £219.00, total £901.00.
- Gas: 12,000 × 6.0p = £720.00, plus 31p × 365 = £113.15, total £833.15.
- Total: £1,734.15.

**Time-of-use (E).** E has two electricity rates, 30p peak and 8p off-peak. Taking the average of the two rates, 19p per kWh, the electricity cost is 3,100 × 19p = £589.00, plus 50p × 365 = £182.50, total £771.50. Gas is on the same terms as V: £833.15. Total: £1,604.65.

**Comparison.**
| Tariff | Annual cost |
| F | £1,938.75 (incl. exit fees) |
| V | £1,734.15 |
| E | £1,604.65 |

E is the cheapest, saving £129.50 a year compared with staying on V, and £334.10 compared with F. On last year's usage, the gap between the cheapest and most expensive option is therefore over £300 a year. Gas costs are identical on V and E, so the whole saving comes from electricity.

**Risk.** V's rates can change with 30 days' notice, so its cost is less certain than E's, which is fixed for 12 months. That reinforces the case for E, since it is both cheaper and locks in prices.

**Recommendation.** Switch to the time-of-use tariff E. The household could increase the saving further by moving more of its electricity use into the off-peak window, for example by timing laundry overnight. Before switching, it should check that its meter can record peak and off-peak use separately, which a time-of-use tariff requires.

flaws.correction: F electricity £960.25; F total £1,813.75 (with no exit fee).

flaws.location: The fixed tariff also carries exit fees of £75 per fuel
flaws.description: The data state that none of the tariffs has an exit fee.
flaws.correction: No exit fees apply. F costs £1,813.75 on last year's usage.

flaws.location: Taking the average of the two rates, 19p per kWh
flaws.description: Uses an unweighted average of peak and off-peak rates instead of weighting by the household's usage (15% off-peak).
flaws.correction: On last year's usage: 2,635 kWh × 30p + 465 kWh × 8p = £827.70, plus £182.50 = £1,010.20; E total £1,843.35. Without the car, E is the most expensive and V (£1,734.15) is cheapest.

flaws.location: Based on last year's usage of 3,100 kWh of electricity and 12,000 kWh of gas
flaws.description: Ignores the electric car arriving next week, which adds about 2,400 kWh of off-peak charging over the year being priced.

open_extensions: Break-even analysis: on base usage alone, E beats V on electricity only if the off-peak share exceeds about 31% (E electricity = £1,112.50 − £682 × share, vs V £901). With 2,400 kWh of car charging the off-peak share rises to (465 + 2,400) / 5,500, about 52%, well above break-even.
Sensitivity to car mileage: E stays cheaper than V as long as off-peak car charging exceeds about 780 kWh a year (the £109.20 E-V gap on base usage divided by the 14p/kWh rate advantage).
Price risk on V: show the bill if V rises by, say, 10% from month 4, to quantify the value of E's 12-month fix.

question: Which production line has the worst defect performance, and did the switch to the new resin supplier on Lines 2 and 3 increase defects?
data:
Injection-moulding plant, three lines making the same part. Four weeks of production.

| Line | Weeks 1-2 units | Weeks 1-2 defects | Weeks 3-4 units | Weeks 3-4 defects |
| Line 1 | 10,000 | 150 | 10,000 | 150 |
| Line 2 | 4,000 | 60 | 4,000 | 140 |
| Line 3 | 6,000 | 90 | 6,000 | 150 |

Changes at the start of week 3:
- Lines 2 and 3 switched to resin from a new supplier. Line 1 stayed on the old resin.
- Lines 2 and 3 also replaced manual sample inspection (1 in 10 parts checked visually, with the defect rate extrapolated to the batch) with 100% automated optical inspection. According to the quality engineer, the optical system detects small surface flaws that the manual check often missed. Line 1 kept manual sampling.

Customer returns traced to each line:
| Line | Weeks 1-2 | Weeks 3-4 |
| Line 1 | 14 | 13 |
| Line 2 | 11 | 12 |
| Line 3 | 9 | 10 |

All three lines run the same shift pattern, with the same staffing levels and a similar mix of operator experience.
draft:
**Defect review: Lines 1-3, weeks 1-4**

**Overview.** Over the four weeks the plant produced 40,000 parts and recorded 740 defects, an overall defect rate of 1.85%. This note looks at which line is performing worst and at the effect of the new resin introduced on Lines 2 and 3 in week 3. All three lines make the same part and run the same shift pattern. Defect rate is defects divided by units produced.

**Line comparison.** Line 1 recorded the most defects (300 over four weeks) and is the line most in need of attention. Line 3 recorded 240 and Line 2 recorded 200. Between them, Lines 2 and 3 produced 20,000 parts, the same as Line 1. Line 1 is also our highest-volume line, so problems there have the biggest impact on output and scrap cost.

**The new resin.** In weeks 1-2 all three lines ran at the same 1.5% defect rate. After the switch, the defect rate on Lines 2 and 3 rose sharply in weeks 3-4, from 1.5% to 3.5% and 2.5% respectively, coinciding with the new resin, while Line 1, which stayed on the old resin, held steady at 1.5%. Line 1 therefore acts as a natural control: whatever else changed in the plant in week 3 affected all lines equally, so the difference must be the resin. Line 2's defect rate more than doubled.

**Customer impact.** The rise is not just an internal measurement issue. Customer returns from Line 2 also roughly doubled after the switch, confirming that more defective parts are reaching customers.

**Line 1.** Line 1's steady 1.5% defect rate reflects the skill and experience of its operators, who have kept quality stable through a period of change elsewhere in the plant. Their practices should be documented and shared with Lines 2 and 3.

**Actions.**
1. Line 1: root-cause review of its defect volume, given it accounts for the largest share of total defects (300 of 740, 41%).
2. Lines 2 and 3: revert to the previous resin supplier immediately and quarantine remaining stock of the new resin.
3. Raise a supplier quality notice with the new resin supplier, including the defect data above.
4. Arrange for Line 1 operators to coach Lines 2 and 3 on handling and settings.
5. Repeat this review after a further four weeks to confirm whether the actions have worked.

**Summary.** Line 1 has the largest defect problem by volume, and the new resin has sharply increased defect rates on the lines where it was introduced.

flaws.location: Line 1 recorded the most defects (300 over four weeks) and is the line most in need of attention
flaws.description: Ranks lines by defect counts, which mostly reflect volume (Line 1 makes half the parts), rather than by defect rate.
flaws.correction: Four-week rates: Line 1 300/20,000 = 1.5%, Line 2 200/8,000 = 2.5%, Line 3 240/12,000 = 2.0%. Line 1 has the lowest rate, not the worst.

flaws.location: the defect rate on Lines 2 and 3 rose sharply in weeks 3-4, from 1.5% to 3.5% and 2.5% respectively, coinciding with the new resin
flaws.description: Ignores that Lines 2 and 3 also switched from 10% manual sampling to 100% automated optical inspection in week 3, which detects flaws the manual check missed. The change did not affect all lines equally, contrary to the 'natural control' argument.
flaws.correction: The rise in recorded defects is confounded with a change in detection. Resin and inspection effects cannot be separated from these data; customer returns (flat) suggest outgoing quality did not worsen.

flaws.location: Customer returns from Line 2 also roughly doubled after the switch
flaws.description: The data show Line 2 returns went from 11 to 12 (and Line 3 from 9 to 10), essentially unchanged.
flaws.correction: Returns were flat on all lines, which supports the detection explanation rather than a real quality decline.

flaws.location: Line 1's steady 1.5% defect rate reflects the skill and experience of its operators
flaws.description: Attributes Line 1's stability to operator skill with no supporting evidence. The data say staffing and experience mix are similar across lines, and Line 1 changed neither resin nor inspection.
flaws.correction: Line 1's stability is explained by it having no process change. Nothing in the data points to operator skill.

open_extensions: Propose a design that separates resin from inspection: run the new resin on one line under the old inspection (or the old resin under the new optical inspection) for two weeks, or re-inspect a retained sample of week 1-2 parts with the optical system to estimate the detection uplift.
Test whether the week 3-4 rises are beyond chance (e.g. Line 2: 60/4,000 vs 140/4,000, two-proportion z of about 5.7), while noting that statistical significance does not resolve the confounding.

Classify defects by type: if the increase is mainly small surface flaws (the kind optical inspection newly catches), that points to detection; if it is short shots or warping, that points to the resin.

question: Which of the two medical wards has the worse 30-day unplanned readmission performance, and does Ward B need a quality-improvement review?
data:
30-day emergency readmissions, two medical wards, financial year 2024-25.

| Ward | Age group | Discharges | Readmitted within 30 days |
| A | Under 75 | 300 | 24 |
| A | 75 and over | 100 | 24 |
| B | Under 75 | 100 | 5 |
| B | 75 and over | 200 | 40 |

Totals: Ward A 400 discharges, 48 readmissions. Ward B 300 discharges, 45 readmissions.

Ward B is the hospital's designated elderly-care ward. Ward A is a general medical ward. Readmission risk rises steeply with age in the hospital's historical data.

Hospital definition: the metric counts unplanned readmissions only. Audit note: Ward B's count above includes 10 planned readmissions (scheduled returns for procedures, all patients aged 75 and over) that were coded incorrectly and should be excluded. Ward A's count has been audited and contains no planned readmissions.

The board's rule of thumb: a ward is referred for a quality-improvement review if its readmission rate is more than 20% (relative) above the comparator ward's.
draft:
**30-day readmissions: Ward A vs Ward B**

**Purpose.** The board asked whether Ward B's readmission performance warrants a quality-improvement (QI) review. Under the board's rule, a ward is referred if its readmission rate is more than 20% higher, in relative terms, than the comparator ward's.

**Definition.** The metric is emergency readmissions within 30 days of discharge, expressed as a percentage of discharges.

**Headline rates.** Ward A discharged 400 patients in 2024-25, of whom 48 were readmitted within 30 days, a rate of 12.0%. Ward B readmitted 45 of its 300 discharged patients within 30 days, a rate of 15.0%.

**Comparison.** Both wards take a similar general medical case mix, so their overall rates can be compared directly without adjustment. Comparing the overall rates, Ward B (15%) is clearly worse than Ward A (12%). The absolute gap is 3 percentage points, which means Ward B's rate is 30% higher than Ward A's. This is well above the board's 20% threshold.

**Scale.** If Ward B had matched Ward A's 12% rate, it would have had 36 readmissions rather than 45, so roughly 9 readmissions a year are attributable to the gap in performance. Across both wards there were 93 readmissions from 700 discharges, 13.3% overall. Each emergency readmission carries both a cost to the hospital and a risk to the patient, so the gap matters in practice.

**Possible drivers.** We have not yet investigated the reasons for Ward B's higher rate. Common contributors include discharge planning, medication reconciliation, follow-up arrangements and communication with community services. A QI review would examine these. Readmission rates are also influenced by factors outside a ward's direct control, including community support after discharge and patients' social circumstances, and the review would need to separate these from factors the ward can influence.

**Proposed scope.** The review would sample a set of Ward B readmissions and examine the discharge summary, medication changes, follow-up arranged, and whether the readmission was for the same condition. It would also gather the views of ward staff and community teams on the discharge process.

**Data.** Both wards' figures cover financial year 2024-25 and use the same 30-day window. Together the two wards discharged 700 patients over the year.

**Recommendation.** Refer Ward B for a QI review, focusing on discharge planning and follow-up. Re-run this comparison at the six-month point to track progress. One year of data is a single snapshot, and rates on a ward with 300 discharges can vary from year to year.

flaws.location: Both wards take a similar general medical case mix
flaws.description: The data say Ward B is the designated elderly-care ward (two-thirds of its discharges are aged 75+, against a quarter of Ward A's), and readmission risk rises steeply with age.
flaws.correction: The case mixes differ sharply. Ward B: 200 of 300 discharges aged 75+; Ward A: 100 of 400.

flaws.location: Comparing the overall rates, Ward B (15%) is clearly worse than Ward A (12%)
flaws.description: Compares crude rates across wards with very different age mixes instead of comparing age-specific (or age-standardised) rates. This is a Simpson's-paradox situation.
flaws.correction: Age-specific rates: under 75, A 8% vs B 5%; 75+, A 24% vs B 20% (15% after the audit correction). Ward B is better in both age groups.

flaws.location: Ward B's rate is 30% higher than Ward A's
flaws.description: 15% / 12% = 1.25, so B's crude rate is 25% higher, not 30%.
flaws.correction: 25% higher on the uncorrected crude figures (still above 20%, but see the omission and method flaws).

flaws.location: Ward B readmitted 45 of its 300 discharged patients within 30 days
flaws.description: Ignores the audit note that 10 of Ward B's 45 readmissions were planned and must be excluded under the hospital definition.
flaws.correction: Unplanned readmissions on Ward B are 35 / 300 = 11.7%, below Ward A's 12.0% even on crude rates. Ward B 75+ becomes 30/200 = 15%. No referral is warranted.

open_extensions: Directly age-standardise to the combined discharge population (400 under 75, 300 aged 75+): Ward A (400×8% + 300×24%) / 700 = 14.9%; Ward B (corrected) (400×5% + 300×15%) / 700 = 9.3%. If anything, Ward A warrants attention.
Report uncertainty: under-75 rates rest on small numbers for Ward B (5 of 100), so give confidence intervals or a stratified (Mantel-Haenszel) comparison before drawing conclusions about Ward A.
Recommend that the audit for planned readmissions be applied routinely to both wards, and check whether other coding issues (e.g. transfers counted as readmissions) differ between wards.

question: By how much did the new fertiliser increase wheat yield in the on-farm trial, is it profitable at current prices, and should the farm business adopt it?
data:
On-farm fertiliser trial, wheat, clay-loam fields, one season. Four field blocks. In each block, one plot received the new fertiliser and an adjacent plot received standard practice (control). Yields in tonnes per hectare (t/ha):

| Block | Control | New fertiliser |
| 1 | 7.2 | 7.9 |
| 2 | 6.8 | 7.3 |
| 3 | 8.1 | 8.5 |
| 4 | 5.9 | 7.6 |

Field log: in June, the Block 4 control plot was waterlogged for about 10 days after a field drain blocked. The Block 4 fertiliser plot, on slightly higher ground, was not affected. No other plots had problems during the season.

Economics:
- The new fertiliser costs £60/ha more than standard practice.
- Grain price: £180 per tonne.
- Application and other costs are the same for both treatments.

The farm business also has sandy-soil holdings in the east of the county, which were not part of the trial. Sandy soils hold less water and nutrients than clay loam.
draft:
**New fertiliser trial: results and recommendation**

**Design.** The trial used four blocks on clay-loam fields, with one plot in each block receiving the new fertiliser and an adjacent plot receiving standard practice. Pairing the plots within blocks controls for differences in soil and drainage between blocks, so the within-block difference is a fair estimate of the fertiliser's effect. Yields were recorded in tonnes per hectare for each plot at harvest.

**Yields.** Average yield was 7.0 t/ha on the control plots and 7.825 t/ha on the fertiliser plots. Control yields ranged from 5.9 to 8.1 t/ha, reflecting differences between blocks; fertiliser yields ranged from 7.3 to 8.5. The fertiliser plots outyielded the control in every block by at least half a tonne per hectare. Within-block gains were 0.7 t/ha (Block 1), 0.5 (Block 2), 0.4 (Block 3) and 1.7 (Block 4).

**Average effect.** Averaging across all four blocks, the fertiliser added 0.825 t/ha. That is a 12% increase on the control yield, which is a substantial gain for a single input change.

**Economics.** At £180/t, the extra grain is worth 0.825 t/ha × £180/t = £168.50 per hectare. Application costs are the same as for standard practice, so the only extra cost is the product itself. Subtracting the additional fertiliser cost of £60/ha leaves a net margin gain of £108.50 per hectare. Across a 400-hectare wheat area this would be worth over £43,000 a year.

**Consistency.** The result is encouraging because the gain appears in every block, which suggests it is not driven by one unusual plot. The largest gain, in Block 4, came on the lowest-yielding block, which is consistent with the fertiliser helping most where conditions are hardest. Block 4 had the lowest control yield, at 5.9 t/ha.

**Scaling up.** Because the effect was consistent across blocks, we can expect a similar gain of around 0.8 t/ha across all our holdings, including the sandy-soil farms in the east.
