**Limitations.** This is a single season, and weather in other years may produce a different response. Four blocks is a small trial, so the average gain carries considerable uncertainty.

**Recommendation.** Adopt the new fertiliser across the farm business from next season, and monitor yields against historical averages to confirm the benefit. We also suggest keeping two of the trial blocks running for a second season to build a longer record, and recording yields by field so that the benefit can be checked against each field's history.

flaws.location: The fertiliser plots outyielded the control in every block by at least half a tonne per hectare
flaws.description: Block 3's gain was 0.4 t/ha (8.5 − 8.1), below half a tonne, as the draft's own next sentence shows.
flaws.correction: Gains ranged from 0.4 to 1.7 t/ha; three of four blocks gained 0.5 t/ha or more.

flaws.location: Averaging across all four blocks, the fertiliser added 0.825 t/ha
flaws.description: Ignores the field-log note that the Block 4 control plot was waterlogged while its paired fertiliser plot was not. This inflates the Block 4 difference (1.7 t/ha) and hence the mean; the draft even reads it as the fertiliser 'helping most where conditions are hardest'.
flaws.correction: Excluding Block 4, the mean gain is (0.7 + 0.5 + 0.4) / 3 = 0.53 t/ha, worth £96/ha, for a net gain of about £36/ha rather than £88.50 (or the draft's £108.50).

flaws.location: 0.825 t/ha × £180/t = £168.50 per hectare
flaws.correction: £148.50/ha gross; net £88.50/ha on all four blocks (about £35,400 on 400 ha, not 'over £43,000').

flaws.location: we can expect a similar gain of around 0.8 t/ha across all our holdings, including the sandy-soil farms in the east
flaws.description: Generalises a one-season, four-block clay-loam result to sandy soils that were not tested and that behave differently.
flaws.correction: The trial supports a (smaller) estimate for clay loam only. Sandy-soil response is unknown and needs its own trial.

open_extensions: Paired t-test: on all four blocks, mean difference 0.825, SD about 0.60, t of about 2.8 on 3 df (p of about 0.07); excluding Block 4, mean 0.53, SD about 0.15, t of about 6.0 on 2 df (p of about 0.03). Note the tiny sample either way.

Break-even yield gain is £60 / £180 = 0.33 t/ha. Even the conservative 0.53 t/ha clears it, but with little margin. Show how the net gain varies with grain price (e.g. at £140/t the conservative estimate nets only about £15/ha).
Recommend a multi-season trial with more blocks and randomised plot positions within blocks, so that drainage or elevation cannot systematically favour one treatment.

question: What effect did the Route 7 fare cut have on ridership and fare revenue in its first quarter, and what does it imply for further fare reductions?
data:
Bus fare trial. From 1 January 2025 the adult single fare on Route 7 was cut from £2.00 to £1.50. Route 9, a similar urban route run by the same operator, kept its £2.00 fare. Neither route changed frequency or timetable.

Boardings (fare-paying adult singles only), January-March:
| Route | Q1 2024 | Q1 2025 |
| Route 7 | 90,000 | 108,000 |
| Route 9 | 80,000 | 92,000 |

City-wide context: a new park-and-ride site and higher city-centre parking charges took effect in October 2024. The operator reports bus use rising across the city since then.

Onboard survey, Route 7, February 2025 (n = 250 passengers who said they began using the route since January). Previous way of making the trip: walked or cycled 51%; drove 22%; used another bus route 18%; did not make the trip 9%.

Fare revenue on Route 7 = boardings × fare.
draft:
**Route 7 fare cut: first-quarter evaluation**

**What changed.** On 1 January 2025 the adult single fare on Route 7 fell from £2.00 to £1.50, a 25% cut. Frequency and timetable were unchanged, so the fare is the only change on the route itself. The boardings figures count fare-paying adult single journeys only and compare January-March 2025 with January-March 2024, so the time of year is matched.

**Ridership.** Route 7's boardings rose 20%, from 90,000 to 108,000, and this increase can be attributed to the fare cut. That is a strong response for a single quarter: Route 7 carried 18,000 more fare-paying adult journeys than a year earlier. Dividing the 20% rise in boardings by the 25% fall in fare gives a fare elasticity of about −0.8.

**Revenue.** Lower fares mean each passenger pays less, but more passengers travel. Fare revenue on Route 7 was £171,000 in Q1 2025 (108,000 × £1.50), down only 5% on the £180,000 of Q1 2024. The extra ridership has therefore recovered most of the revenue that the fare cut would otherwise have cost, which makes the scheme close to self-financing. Revenue here covers adult single fares only, since other ticket types are not in the data.

**Who are the new riders?** The onboard survey asked 250 passengers who started using Route 7 since January how they used to make the trip. More than half of new riders previously drove, which suggests the fare cut is taking cars off the road and should help with congestion and emissions on the corridor.

**Implications for further cuts.** The response gives us a basis for estimating the effect of deeper cuts. With an elasticity of −0.8, a 100% fare reduction would lift ridership by about 80%, so making the route free would increase ridership by around 80%. A free route would of course remove fare revenue entirely, so this would need to be weighed against the congestion and emissions benefits.

**Caveats.** One quarter is a short period, and some of the early response may reflect novelty or publicity around the cut. The survey covered only passengers who said they began using the route since January. Route 9, with no fare change, is a useful point of reference for future monitoring.

**Recommendation.** Make the Route 7 fare permanent, consider extending the £1.50 fare to similar routes, and model a free-fare pilot using the elasticity above. Boardings should continue to be collected monthly, and the onboard survey repeated in six months, so that the longer-run response can be tracked.

flaws.location: Route 7's boardings rose 20%, from 90,000 to 108,000, and this increase can be attributed to the fare cut
flaws.description: Ignores the comparison route: Route 9, with no fare change, grew 15% over the same period (and city-wide bus use was rising). The baseline trend must be removed.
flaws.correction: Relative to Route 9, Route 7 grew 1.20/1.15 − 1 = about 4.3% (5 points by difference-in-differences). Implied elasticity is roughly −0.17 to −0.2, not −0.8.

flaws.location: Fare revenue on Route 7 was £171,000 in Q1 2025 (108,000 × £1.50), down only 5%
flaws.correction: Revenue fell from £180,000 to £162,000, a 10% fall. The scheme is far from self-financing.

flaws.location: More than half of new riders previously drove
flaws.description: The survey says 22% previously drove; 51% previously walked or cycled.
flaws.correction: About one in five new riders switched from the car. Most new riders came from walking/cycling or other bus routes, so congestion benefits are modest.

flaws.location: making the route free would increase ridership by around 80%
flaws.description: Extrapolates a single elasticity estimate linearly far outside the observed range (to a 100% fare cut). The estimate itself is inflated by the baseline error.
flaws.correction: The data say nothing reliable about a free fare. Responses to zero fares are not linear extrapolations of small cuts.

open_extensions: Cost per additional trip: without the cut, Route 7 would be expected to carry about 90,000 × 1.15 = 103,500 boardings, earning £207,000 at £2.00. The cut added about 4,500 boardings and reduced revenue to £162,000, a cost of about £45,000, or roughly £10 per additional trip.
Use the survey's 18% 'used another bus route' to note that some growth is displacement from other routes, so the network-wide ridership gain is smaller than the route-level one.
Ask for monthly data: if the novelty effect is real, the gap between Routes 7 and 9 should narrow over January-March; a longer series (Q2-Q4) would firm up the elasticity.

question: Did the spring 15%-off loyalty email campaign pay off, and should the company repeat it (or extend it to non-member customers)?
data:
Spring loyalty email: '15% off everything for 14 days'. Loyalty members were randomly split: 50,000 received the email and 10,000 were held out (no email). Outcomes over the 14 days:

| Group | Members | Purchasers | Revenue (after discount) | Contribution |
| Emailed | 50,000 | 3,000 | £180,000 | £36,000 |
| Holdout | 10,000 | 500 | £35,000 | £10,500 |

Contribution = revenue after discount minus cost of goods and fulfilment. Revenue and contribution cover all purchases made in the 14-day window; purchasers are members who bought at least once in it.

Emailed members who purchased could redeem the 15% discount on everything they bought, including items they would have bought anyway. Holdout members paid full price.

Campaign sending cost: £2,000 (copywriting, design and email platform fees).

Loyalty members are the company's most engaged customers. Non-members make up 70% of the customer base and have never been sent a discount offer; they buy less often and have lower average basket values.
draft:
**Spring loyalty email: campaign evaluation**

**Background.** The spring campaign offered loyalty members 15% off everything for 14 days, delivered by email.

**Design.** The campaign was evaluated with a randomised holdout: 50,000 loyalty members received the 15%-off email and 10,000 were held back. Because the holdout was drawn at random from the same loyalty list, the two groups should be alike in every respect other than receiving the email, so the holdout tells us what emailed members would have done without it.

**Conversion.** 6.0% of emailed members made a purchase (3,000 of 50,000), against 5.0% of the holdout (500 of 10,000). At the holdout's 5.0% rate we would have expected 2,500 purchasers rather than 3,000. That is a 1.0-point lift, or a 10% relative lift in purchase rate. The difference is comfortably significant given the sample sizes.

**Revenue.** Revenue per emailed member was £3.60 against £3.50 in the holdout, so the email lifted revenue by about £5,000 across the 50,000 members. Average order value was £60 for emailed purchasers and £70 for holdout purchasers, consistent with the discount reducing the price of each basket. Total revenue across both groups was £215,000.

**Return on investment.** The campaign generated £180,000 of revenue for £2,000 of sending cost, a return of 89 to 1. Very few marketing activities come close to that, and at 4p per emailed member the cost is low enough that even a much weaker response would still pay back.

**Measurement.** All results cover the 14-day offer window only. Purchases after the window closed are not included, so any longer-term effect on loyalty, positive or negative, is not captured here.

**Segments.** The results are reported for the loyalty base as a whole. Splitting by how recently members last purchased, or by their usual spend, could show where the offer worked best and help target future campaigns.

**Extending the offer.** Non-members make up 70% of our customer base and have never received a discount email. Given the response from members, the same offer sent to our non-member customers should lift their purchase rate by a similar proportion, which would be a significant opportunity given the size of that group.

**Recommendation.**
1. Repeat the loyalty campaign quarterly.
2. Pilot the same 15%-off email to non-members next quarter.
3. Keep a holdout in future campaigns so that we can keep measuring the lift.
4. Share these results with the trading team so that future offers are planned against a measured baseline.

flaws.location: a 10% relative lift in purchase rate
flaws.description: A rise from 5.0% to 6.0% is a 20% relative lift (1.0 / 5.0), not 10%.
flaws.correction: Relative lift = 20%.

flaws.location: The campaign generated £180,000 of revenue for £2,000 of sending cost, a return of 89 to 1
flaws.description: Attributes all revenue from emailed members to the email, ignoring the holdout baseline, which the draft itself has just used. Most of the £180,000 would have been earned anyway.
flaws.correction: Incremental revenue is (£3.60 − £3.50) × 50,000 = about £5,000, i.e. about 2.5 times the sending cost on revenue (before costs of goods), not 89 to 1.

flaws.location: Revenue per emailed member was £3.60 against £3.50 in the holdout, so the email lifted revenue by about £5,000 across the 50,000 members
flaws.description: Ignores the contribution data. Because the discount applied to purchases members would have made anyway, contribution per member fell.
flaws.correction: Contribution per member: emailed £36,000 / 50,000 = £0.72 vs holdout £10,500 / 10,000 = £1.05. Expected without the email: £52,500, so contribution fell by about £16,500, or about £18,500 after sending costs. The campaign lost money and should not be repeated as designed.

flaws.location: the same offer sent to our non-member customers should lift their purchase rate by a similar proportion
flaws.description: Generalises from the most engaged customer segment to a different population that has never received offers and behaves differently.
flaws.correction: No estimate for non-members is supported. A pilot with its own holdout would be needed, and it should be judged on contribution, not revenue.

open_extensions: Test whether the conversion difference is statistically reliable: 6.0% vs 5.0% with n = 50,000 and 10,000 gives z of about 3.9, so the purchase-rate lift is real even though the campaign is unprofitable.

Decompose the contribution loss into a subsidy on baseline purchases versus margin on incremental purchases, and find the break-even discount depth (or a threshold offer such as '15% off over £80') that would make the campaign pay.
Look beyond the 14-day window: check whether emailed members bought less in the following weeks (pull-forward), which would make the true incremental effect even smaller.

question: Which team has the highest staff turnover, and is remote-first working associated with lower turnover?
data:
Annual staff turnover, three teams, calendar year 2025.

| Team | Working model | Headcount 1 Jan | Headcount 31 Dec | Average headcount | Leavers in year |
| A | Remote-first | 30 | 70 | 50 | 6 |
| B | Office-based | 120 | 120 | 120 | 18 |
| C | Hybrid | 80 | 80 | 80 | 8 |

HR convention: annual turnover rate = leavers / average headcount over the year.

Team B's 18 leavers include 10 fixed-term contract staff (a 12-month project team) whose contracts ended as planned in June. The other 8 were voluntary resignations. All leavers in Teams A and C were voluntary resignations. The company's attrition target relates to voluntary turnover.

Team A was created in 2024 and grew through 2025; most of its staff have less than a year's service.

Exit interviews (all 32 leavers), main reason given: pay 10; end of fixed-term contract 10; career progression 7; relocation 5.
draft:
**Staff turnover by team, 2025**

**Data.** The figures cover calendar year 2025 for the three teams, with headcount recorded at 1 January and 31 December and leavers counted over the year.

**Context.** Team A is the newest team: it was set up in 2024 and more than doubled in size during 2025, from 30 to 70 people. Team B is the largest team.

**Method.** Turnover has been calculated for each team as leavers divided by headcount, using each team's end-of-year headcount as the base, since that reflects the current size of the team.

**Results.**
- Team A (remote-first): 6 leavers on a headcount of 70, a turnover rate of 8.6%.
- Team B (office-based): 18 leavers on a headcount of 120, 15.0%.
- Team C (hybrid): 8 leavers on a headcount of 80, 10.0%.

Team B has the highest turnover by a clear margin, at 15.0%, and Team A the lowest. Teams B and C were the same size at the start and end of the year; only Team A changed size. Company-wide, 32 people left during the year.

**Working model.** The ranking lines up exactly with the working model: remote-first lowest, hybrid in the middle, office-based highest. Team C, which is hybrid, sits between the other two. Remote-first working clearly reduces turnover, and moving Teams B and C to remote-first should bring their turnover down towards Team A's level. Applied to Team B alone, cutting turnover from 15.0% to around 8.6% would mean roughly 8 fewer leavers a year.

**Reasons for leaving.** Exit interviews give a clear picture of why people leave: a majority of leavers cited pay as the main reason. Career progression and relocation were the other main reasons given. All 32 leavers completed an exit interview, so the picture is complete. This suggests that, alongside working-model changes, a pay benchmarking exercise is needed.

**Team B.** Team B's high turnover is a concern, because it is the largest team and replacing staff is costly. Its 18 leavers account for more than half of all leavers across the company. Each departure carries recruitment, onboarding and lost-productivity costs, so even modest reductions are worth pursuing. We recommend a retention review for Team B, including stay interviews with current staff.

**Recommendations.**
1. Pilot remote-first working in Team B from next quarter.
2. Commission a pay benchmarking review across all three teams.
3. Track turnover quarterly by team, using the method above.
4. Repeat the exit-interview analysis each quarter so that trends in reasons for leaving can be followed.

flaws.location: using each team's end-of-year headcount as the base
flaws.description: Uses year-end headcount as the denominator instead of average headcount (the HR convention). This matters for Team A, which grew from 30 to 70.
flaws.correction: Team A: 6 / 50 = 12.0% (not 8.6%). Teams B and C are unchanged (15.0% and 10.0%). On all leavers, Team C is lowest, not Team A.

flaws.location: Team B (office-based): 18 leavers on a headcount of 120, 15.0%
flaws.description: Ignores that 10 of Team B's 18 leavers were fixed-term contracts ending as planned, not voluntary turnover (the target metric).
flaws.correction: Voluntary turnover: A 12.0%, B 8/120 = 6.7%, C 10.0%. Team B has the lowest voluntary turnover and the remote-first team the highest.

flaws.location: Remote-first working clearly reduces turnover
flaws.description: Draws a causal conclusion about working models from three teams that differ in many ways (Team A is new, fast-growing and short-tenured). Corrected, the ranking does not even hold.
flaws.correction: Three teams cannot establish an effect of working model. On corrected figures remote-first has the highest voluntary turnover, which is also consistent with its short tenure.

flaws.location: a majority of leavers cited pay as the main reason
flaws.description: 10 of 32 leavers (31%) cited pay, not a majority; 10 cited the planned end of a contract.
flaws.correction: Pay was cited by 10 of 32 leavers (31%), or 10 of 22 voluntary leavers (45%). It is the most common voluntary reason, but not a majority.

open_extensions: Report company-wide turnover properly: all leavers 32/250 = 12.8%, voluntary 22/250 = 8.8% (average headcount 250).
Control for tenure: compare first-year leaving rates across teams, since turnover is typically highest in the first year and Team A is mostly first-year staff.
With small counts (6, 8 and 8 voluntary leavers), give confidence intervals or note that differences of a few percentage points between teams are within noise.

question: Are young drivers on telematics policies lower risk than those on standard policies, and would making telematics compulsory for all young drivers reduce claims?
data:
Motor insurer, drivers aged 18-24, policy year 2025. Telematics ('black box') policies are optional: customers choose them in exchange for a discount.

| | Telematics | Standard |
| Policies (full-year equivalent) | 4,000 | 6,000 |
| Claims | 360 | 780 |
| Average cost per claim | £3,200 | £3,500 |
| Average annual premium | £1,100 | £1,400 |
| Average annual mileage | 6,000 | 9,500 |

Loss ratio = total claims cost / total premium. Premiums shown are after any telematics discount. Average cost per claim includes settled and reserved amounts. All policies are for private cars.

Mileage for telematics policies is measured by the device. Mileage for standard policies is customer-declared at renewal; the insurer's audits find declarations accurate to within 5% on average.

The pricing team wants to know whether telematics customers are lower risk, and whether making telematics compulsory for all young drivers would reduce claims.
draft:
**Telematics vs standard policies: young drivers, 2025**

**Data.** The analysis covers full-year-equivalent policies for drivers aged 18-24 in 2025, comparing 4,000 telematics policies with 6,000 standard policies. Premiums shown are after the telematics discount.

**Claim frequency.** Telematics drivers had 360 claims across 4,000 policies, 9.0 claims per 100 policies. Standard-policy drivers had 780 claims across 6,000 policies, 13.0 per 100. Across both books there were 1,140 claims on 10,000 policies, 11.4 per 100. In other words, telematics drivers make 31% fewer claims per policy (9.0 vs 13.0 claims per 100 policies), a large and commercially important difference.

**Claim severity.** Claim severity is broadly similar in the two groups, at about £3,500 per claim, so the difference in risk comes almost entirely from how often telematics drivers claim rather than how much each claim costs.

**Profitability.** Telematics premiums are lower, averaging £1,100 against £1,400, because of the discount. Despite that, telematics claims cost £1.152m against £4.4m of premium, a loss ratio of 22.6%. Standard policies have claims of £2.73m against £8.4m of premium, a loss ratio of 32.5%. Telematics business is therefore more profitable per pound of premium, even after the discount. Total premium across both books was £12.8m. Claims cost per policy was £288 for telematics and £455 for standard. Young drivers are the highest-risk age group in motor insurance, so differences in claims experience have a large effect on profitability.

**Why the difference?** The device gives drivers feedback on speed, braking and night driving, and drivers know their behaviour is being monitored. It is plausible that this encourages safer driving.

**Compulsory telematics.** The evidence supports extending telematics. Making telematics compulsory for all young drivers would cut their claim frequency by around 31%, bringing the standard book's 13.0 claims per 100 policies down to about 9.0. On 6,000 policies that is about 240 fewer claims a year.

**Implementation.** Compulsory telematics would need changes to the sales process, device supply and installation, and customer communications. The discount structure would also need redesigning, since there would no longer be a choice to reward.

**Recommendation.** Move to compulsory telematics for all new policies for drivers aged 18-24 from next year, and review the size of the telematics discount, which on these figures could be reduced without making the product uncompetitive. Any change to the discount should be tested on new business first, so that its effect on take-up can be measured. Claim frequency, severity and loss ratio should be tracked quarterly for both books.

flaws.location: telematics drivers make 31% fewer claims per policy (9.0 vs 13.0 claims per 100 policies)
flaws.description: Ignores exposure: telematics drivers drive far less (6,000 vs 9,500 miles a year). Per-policy frequency mostly reflects mileage.
flaws.correction: Claims per million miles: telematics 360 / 24m = 15.0; standard 780 / 57m = 13.7. Per mile driven, telematics drivers claim slightly more often.

flaws.location: Claim severity is broadly similar in the two groups, at about £3,500 per claim
flaws.description: The data give £3,200 per claim for telematics and £3,500 for standard.
flaws.correction: Telematics claims are about 9% cheaper on average, so severity also differs.

flaws.location: a loss ratio of 22.6%
flaws.correction: Telematics loss ratio 26.2% vs standard 32.5%.

flaws.location: Making telematics compulsory for all young drivers would cut their claim frequency by around 31%
flaws.description: Treats a difference between self-selected groups as a causal effect of the device. Customers who chose telematics differ (e.g. they drive much less), and compulsion changes who is in the group.
flaws.correction: The data cannot estimate the effect of compulsion. Given the per-mile comparison, much or all of the gap is selection on mileage. A randomised or staggered rollout would be needed.

open_extensions: Mileage-adjusted pricing check: telematics premium per 1,000 miles is £183 vs £147 for standard, and claims cost per 1,000 miles is £48 vs £48, so on a per-mile basis the two books are similar in risk.

Sensitivity to declared mileage: even if standard drivers under-declare by 5%, per-mile frequency becomes about 13.0 per million miles for standard vs 15.0 for telematics, so the conclusion is robust.

Within the telematics book, relate device-measured driving scores (speeding, harsh braking, night driving) to claims. That tests the behaviour-change mechanism directly rather than through a self-selected comparison.

question: Under company policy, which of the five stores should receive this year's refurbishment budget?
data:
Five-store retail chain, financial year 2025. A refurbishment budget is available for one store. Company policy: the budget goes to the store with the lowest annual sales per square foot of sales floor (the company's space-productivity KPI), measured on a full-year basis.

| Store | Annual sales 2025 | Sales floor area (sq ft) | Gross internal area incl. stockrooms (sq ft) |
| North | £2.4m | 8,000 | 10,000 |
| South | £3.6m | 15,000 | 18,000 |
| East | £1.8m | 6,000 | 9,000 |
| West | £2.1m | 10,000 | 12,000 |
| Central | £4.2m | 12,000 | 14,000 |

Annual sales 2024: North £2.3m, South £3.5m, East £1.7m, West £2.9m, Central £4.0m. Floor areas were the same in 2024.

Operations note: West was closed from January to March 2025 (3 months) for flood repairs, so its 2025 sales cover 9 trading months. All other stores traded for all 12 months in both years. The flood repairs were covered by insurance and did not change the store's layout.
draft:
**Refurbishment budget: store productivity review**

**Approach.** Policy is to allocate the refurbishment budget to the store with the lowest sales per square foot. I have used gross internal area, including stockrooms, as the denominator, because it reflects the full space each store occupies and pays rent on, and so gives a fuller picture of space productivity.

**Data.** Sales figures are for financial year 2025, with 2024 figures for comparison. Floor areas were the same in both years.

**Sales density, 2025.**
| Store | Sales | Gross area | Sales per sq ft |
| North | £2.4m | 10,000 | £240 |
| South | £3.6m | 18,000 | £200 |
| East | £1.8m | 9,000 | £200 |
| West | £2.1m | 12,000 | £175 |
| Central | £4.2m | 14,000 | £320 |

**Ranking.** Central is the most productive store by a wide margin, at £320 per square foot, roughly 60% above South and East. North sits in the middle. South and East are tied at £200. West is the clear lowest at £175 per square foot, some 12.5% below the next-weakest stores.

**Trend.** This is not a one-year blip. West was also the weakest store last year, and its sales have fallen from £2.9m to £2.1m, a drop of more than a quarter. The combination of the lowest density and a steep decline makes West the obvious priority.

**Other considerations.** The other stores all grew sales between 2024 and 2025: North by 4%, South by 3%, East by 6% and Central by 5%. Total chain sales were £14.1m in 2025, against £14.4m in 2024. The growth elsewhere suggests the chain's offer is broadly working, and West's problem is local, which a refurbishment is well placed to address. If West's weakness proves to reflect local trading conditions rather than the store itself, a refurbishment alone may not fix it, so a short review of its catchment should accompany the works.

**Recommendation.** Allocate this year's refurbishment budget to West. Review its sales density twelve months after the works to measure the return on the investment.

**Measuring the result.** Post-refurbishment sales density should be compared with the store's previous level and with the rest of the chain over the same period, so that chain-wide trends are not mistaken for the effect of the works. The store will need to close or trade partially during the works, so timing should avoid peak trading periods.

flaws.location: I have used gross internal area, including stockrooms, as the denominator
flaws.description: The company KPI is sales per square foot of sales floor, not gross internal area. Using gross area changes the densities and their relative gaps.
flaws.correction: Sales-floor densities (2025 as reported): North £300, South £240, East £300, West £210, Central £350.

flaws.description: £4.2m / 14,000 = £300, not £320 (even on the draft's gross-area basis).
flaws.correction: £300 per sq ft gross (or £350 on sales floor). Central is 50%, not 'roughly 60%', above South and East on gross area.

flaws.location: West is the clear lowest at £175 per square foot
flaws.description: Ignores that West traded for only 9 months in 2025 (flood closure), while policy requires a full-year basis.
flaws.correction: Annualised West sales = £2.1m × 12/9 = £2.8m: £280 per sq ft of sales floor. The lowest full-year density is South at £240, so South gets the budget.

flaws.location: West was also the weakest store last year
flaws.description: In 2024 West had the second-highest density (£2.9m / 10,000 = £290 per sq ft of sales floor). South was the weakest (£3.5m / 15,000 = £233).
flaws.correction: West was not weak in 2024. Its 2025 'decline' is the closure, so there is no trend case for West; South was weakest in both years.

open_extensions: Show the decision is robust: South is lowest on sales-floor density in both 2024 (£233) and annualised 2025 (£240), while on gross area South and East tie at £200 once West is annualised (£233), which shows why the KPI's definition matters.
Check West's post-reopening run rate (monthly sales April-December vs the same months of 2024) to confirm that annualising is fair, i.e. that West did not reopen with depressed trade.
Consider return on refurbishment rather than lowest density alone: e.g. South's large floor (15,000 sq ft) means each £10/sq ft uplift is worth £150,000 a year, more than in any other store.

question: Did the 1 June move to a new content delivery network (CDN) improve the site's conversion rate, and what is a faster site worth?
data:
An online retailer migrated its website to a new content delivery network (CDN) on 1 June. Two weeks before (18-31 May) vs two weeks after (1-14 June):

| Metric | 18-31 May | 1-14 June |
| Sessions | 200,000 | 210,000 |
| Orders | 5,000 | 5,670 |
| Median page load time | 3.2 s | 2.1 s |
| 95th-percentile page load time | 7.5 s | 4.8 s |
| Bounce rate | 48% | 44% |

Conversion = orders / sessions. Page load times come from real-user monitoring across all page views.

Same two calendar periods last year, when there were no site or infrastructure changes: conversion 2.4% (18-31 May) and 2.6% (1-14 June).

The retailer's conversion rate rises every year in early June when the summer ranges launch. This year the summer ranges again launched on 1 June. No other site changes were made between 18 May and 14 June.
draft:
**CDN migration: performance and conversion impact**

**Background.** The site moved to a new CDN on 1 June. This note compares the two weeks before the migration (18-31 May) with the two weeks after (1-14 June). Load times come from real-user monitoring, so they reflect what customers experienced on their own devices and connections. The analysis uses site-wide totals; device and channel splits are not included.

**Speed.** The migration delivered a large improvement in page speed. Median page load time fell from 3.2 seconds to 2.1 seconds, a 34% reduction. The slowest experiences improved even more: the 95th-percentile load time fell from 7.5 to 4.8 seconds, so the 95th-percentile load time fell by 56%. This matters because the slowest page loads are the ones most likely to drive customers away. Median load time is now 2.1 seconds, and 95% of page loads complete within 4.8 seconds.

**Engagement.** Bounce rate fell by a third, from 48% to 32%, indicating that far fewer visitors are leaving after a single page (bounce rate is the share of sessions that view only one page). Sessions also grew, from 200,000 to 210,000 (5%), and orders from 5,000 to 5,670 (13%).

**Conversion.** Conversion rose from 2.50% (5,000 orders from 200,000 sessions) to 2.70% (5,670 from 210,000), a gain of 0.2 points that we attribute to the faster site. No other site changes were made in the period, so the CDN is the only candidate explanation on the site side. In relative terms the gain is 8%, and at current volumes it is worth roughly 420 extra orders a fortnight (0.2% of 210,000 sessions). Orders per day rose from about 357 to 405.

**What is a second worth?** Median load time fell by 1.1 seconds and conversion rose by 0.2 points, so each second of load time is worth about 0.18 points of conversion, and a further one-second improvement would add another 0.18 points. This gives us a simple rule for prioritising future performance work against other projects.

**Next steps.**
1. Prioritise further speed work, starting with image optimisation on product pages, with a target of a 1.1-second median load time.
2. Use the 0.18-points-per-second figure in business cases for performance projects.
3. Continue monitoring load times and conversion weekly. Two weeks is a short window, and we should confirm that the speed improvement holds as traffic grows over the summer.

**Conclusion.** The CDN migration made the site substantially faster and lifted conversion by 0.2 points.

flaws.location: so the 95th-percentile load time fell by 56%
flaws.description: The reduction is (7.5 − 4.8) / 7.5 = 36%. 56% comes from dividing the 2.7 s fall by the new value (4.8). The draft's claim that the slowest experiences 'improved even more' than the median (34%) is barely true at 36%.
flaws.correction: 95th percentile fell by 36%, similar to the median's 34%.

flaws.location: Bounce rate fell by a third, from 48% to 32%
flaws.description: The data show bounce rate fell from 48% to 44%.
flaws.correction: A 4-point (8% relative) fall in bounce rate.

flaws.location: a gain of 0.2 points that we attribute to the faster site
flaws.description: Ignores the seasonal baseline: the same calendar periods last year, with no site changes, show the same 0.2-point rise (2.4% to 2.6%) from the summer range launch, which happened again on 1 June.
flaws.correction: Year-over-year difference-in-differences: (2.70 − 2.50) − (2.6 − 2.4) = 0.0 points. There is no detectable conversion effect of the CDN.

flaws.location: each second of load time is worth about 0.18 points of conversion, and a further one-second improvement would add another 0.18 points
flaws.description: Derives a linear causal 'value per second' from one confounded before/after comparison and extrapolates it beyond the observed range.
flaws.correction: The data support no value-per-second estimate (the seasonally adjusted effect is about zero). A randomised latency experiment would be needed.

open_extensions: Run a statistical check on the raw conversion change (2.50% vs 2.70%, z of about 4) and contrast it with the seasonally adjusted comparison, showing that a highly significant before/after change can be entirely seasonal.
Check whether the sessions increase (+5%) is also seasonal, using last year's session counts for the same periods, which the analyst should request.
Segment by device or connection type: speed gains typically matter most on mobile and slow connections, so an effect masked in the aggregate could appear there (data would be needed).

question: Which appeal letter, A (personal story) or B (impact statistics), should the charity use for its next mailing to previous donors?
data:
Spring appeal. 40,000 previous donors were randomly split between two letters.

| Letter | Sent | Gifts | Total raised |
| A (personal story) | 20,000 | 1,000 | £40,000 |
| B (impact statistics) | 20,000 | 800 | £44,000 |

Print and postage: £0.60 per letter for both versions. Both letters were posted on the same day and gave the same reply deadline. Each responding donor made one gift.

Note from the major-gifts team: Letter B's total includes a single gift of £8,000 from a long-standing major donor, who has given between £5,000 and £10,000 to every spring appeal for nine years, whichever letter they received. No gift to Letter A exceeded £500, and no other gift to Letter B exceeded £500.

The next mailing will go to a similar pool of previous donors. The charity's other materials (website, legacy brochure, event packs) are aimed at different audiences, including people who have never donated.
draft:
**Spring appeal: Letter A vs Letter B**

**Design.** 40,000 previous donors were randomly split into two equal groups. Group A received a letter built around a personal story, and group B received one built around impact statistics. Random allocation means differences in response can be attributed to the letters.

**Background.** The test was large, with 20,000 donors per letter, so chance differences between the groups should be small. Both letters were posted on the same day with the same deadline, so timing does not differ between them. The next mailing goes to a similar pool of previous donors, so this test is directly relevant to it.

**Response rate.** Letter A produced 1,000 gifts from 20,000 letters (5.0%), and Letter B produced 800 (4.0%). More people responded to the story: Letter A's response rate was 25% higher than Letter B's, and it brought in 200 more gifts. Each version went to 20,000 donors, and response rate here means gifts divided by letters sent.

**Gift size.** Letter B raised £44,000 from 800 gifts, an average of £55. Letter A raised £40,000 from 1,000 gifts, an average of £40. Letter B's average is therefore £15 higher.

**Which letter performed better?** The key question for a fundraising letter is how much each donor gives. Letter B's average gift was £55 against £40 for Letter A, so B is the more effective letter. In total, B raised 15% more than A from the same number of letters.

**Costs.** Both letters cost £0.60 each to print and post, £12,000 per version. Together the two versions cost £24,000 and raised £84,000. After costs, A netted £28,000 and B £32,000. The cost per gift was £12 for Letter A and £15 for Letter B.

**Interpretation.** The pattern is clear: fewer people gave to Letter B, but those who did gave substantially more, 37.5% more per gift on average. Donors respond better to statistics than to stories when deciding how much to give, so we should rewrite the website, legacy brochure and event materials in the impact-statistics style as well.

**Recommendation.** Use Letter B for the next mailing to previous donors, and begin revising the charity's other materials in the same style. Future appeals should keep a randomised split so the charity continues to learn what works; a useful next test would compare Letter B with a version that combines a story with headline statistics. Future tests could also check whether the letters perform differently for recent and lapsed donors.

flaws.location: Letter B's average gift was £55 against £40 for Letter A, so B is the more effective letter
flaws.description: Chooses on average gift size alone, ignoring response rate. The right metric for a mailing is net income per letter sent (response rate × average gift − cost).
flaws.correction: Income per letter: A £2.00, B £2.20 on raw totals (B £1.80 without the major gift); the response-rate gap must be weighed, not ignored.

flaws.location: B raised 15% more than A
flaws.correction: 10% more on raw totals.

flaws.location: Letter B raised £44,000 from 800 gifts, an average of £55
flaws.description: Ignores the £8,000 gift from a major donor who gives every year regardless of the letter. It is not a response to Letter B and dominates the comparison.
flaws.correction: Excluding it: B raised £36,000 from 799 gifts (average about £45), £1.80 per letter, net £24,000 vs A's £28,000. Letter A is better.

flaws.location: Donors respond better to statistics than to stories when deciding how much to give, so we should rewrite the website, legacy brochure and event materials
flaws.description: Generalises a single mailing test on previous donors to different materials and audiences (including people who have never donated), and the underlying finding disappears once the major gift is removed.
flaws.correction: The test supports, at most, a choice of letter for previous donors (A). It says nothing about other channels or audiences.

open_extensions: Test the response-rate difference: 5.0% vs 4.0% on 20,000 each gives z of about 4.8, so the higher response to A is very unlikely to be chance.
Compare gift-size distributions without the outlier (e.g. medians, or a trimmed mean), since a single large gift can swing averages; ask for gift-level data.

Consider long-run value: A recruits 200 more donor responses, which may raise retention and future giving. A lifetime-value comparison, using the charity's repeat-giving rates, would strengthen the case.

question: How much did the average-speed cameras reduce injury collisions at the 10 sites, and what would a city-wide rollout achieve?
data:
Average-speed cameras at 10 sites, installed January 2023. The 10 sites were chosen because they had the highest numbers of injury collisions in the city in 2020-2022.

| | 2020-2022 (3 years before) | 2023-2025 (3 years after) |
| Injury collisions at the 10 camera sites | 156 | 102 |
| Injury collisions on all other city roads | 3,600 | 3,240 |

Traffic: a bypass opened in March 2023 and diverted through-traffic away from 6 of the 10 sites. Traffic counts at the 10 sites fell by an average of 15% between the two periods. Traffic on other city roads was broadly unchanged.

Speed surveys at the camera sites (speed limit 30 mph): mean speed 34 mph before installation, 31 mph after.

The 10 sites are all urban arterial roads. The city has about 900 km of roads, of which the camera sites cover about 12 km. Most of the network is residential streets with low collision counts.
draft:
**Average-speed cameras: three-year evaluation**

**Background.** Average-speed cameras were installed at 10 sites in January 2023. This note compares injury collisions in the three years before (2020-2022) and after (2023-2025) installation, at the 10 sites and on all other city roads. All 10 sites are urban arterial roads, together covering about 12 km of the city's 900 km road network, about 1.3% of its length. The before and after periods are both three full years, so the comparison is balanced in length.

**Site selection.** Because the sites were the city's worst collision hotspots in 2020-2022, they were the right place to start, and the 2020-2022 period gives a fair baseline for judging the cameras' effect at those sites.

**Raw change.** Injury collisions at the 10 sites fell from 156 to 102, from an average of 52 a year to 34 a year, a fall of 35%. That is 54 fewer injury collisions over three years.

**Allowing for the background trend.** Collisions also fell on other city roads, from 3,600 to 3,240 (10%). Relative to that trend, the camera sites' reduction is about 27% (other roads went from an average of 1,200 collisions a year to 1,080): the ratio of after to before at the sites (0.654) divided by the same ratio on other roads (0.900) is 0.727. Applying the background 10% fall to the sites' before-period rate gives an expected 46.8 collisions a year without cameras, against 34 observed, so the cameras prevented about 13 injury collisions a year at these sites.

**Mechanism.** Speed surveys support this. Mean speeds at the camera sites fell from 34 mph to 26 mph, taking typical speeds well below the 30 mph limit. Lower speeds reduce both the chance of a collision and its severity, so this is the mechanism we would expect.

**City-wide rollout.** The results make a strong case for wider use. Rolling cameras out across the whole city road network would therefore cut injury collisions by around 27%, which on current figures would prevent roughly 290 injury collisions a year on other roads (27% of 1,080).

**Recommendation.** Fund a city-wide programme of average-speed cameras, prioritising roads with the highest collision counts, and continue to monitor collisions annually at the original 10 sites.

**Costs.** Average-speed camera systems carry installation, maintenance and enforcement costs, which a full business case for wider rollout would need to set against the value of collisions prevented. The evaluation should also be published so that residents can see the results.

flaws.location: the 2020-2022 period gives a fair baseline for judging the cameras' effect at those sites
flaws.description: Ignores regression to the mean. The sites were selected because their 2020-2022 counts were the highest, so that period is likely inflated by chance, and counts would be expected to fall even without cameras.
flaws.correction: The before period overstates the true underlying rate. An RTM adjustment (e.g. an empirical-Bayes estimate using longer histories or comparable sites) is needed, and the 27% figure is an upper bound.

flaws.location: the cameras prevented about 13 injury collisions a year at these sites
flaws.description: Ignores the 15% fall in traffic at the sites after the bypass opened, which would reduce collisions on its own.
flaws.correction: Expected without cameras, allowing for trend and traffic: 52 × 0.90 × 0.85 = 39.8 a year, so about 6 prevented a year (roughly a 15% relative reduction), before any RTM adjustment.

flaws.location: Mean speeds at the camera sites fell from 34 mph to 26 mph
flaws.description: The surveys show mean speed fell from 34 to 31 mph, still above the 30 mph limit.
flaws.correction: A 3 mph fall in mean speed; speeds remain slightly above the limit.

flaws.location: Rolling cameras out across the whole city road network would therefore cut injury collisions by around 27%
flaws.description: Generalises from 12 km of the highest-collision arterial roads to 900 km of mostly low-collision residential streets, with a selection-inflated effect estimate.
flaws.correction: No city-wide estimate is supported. The effect on typical roads, which have low counts, would be much smaller in absolute terms and is unknown in relative terms.

open_extensions: Request each site's collision counts for earlier years (e.g. 2015-2019) to estimate the regression-to-the-mean component directly.
Split the 10 sites into the 6 affected by the bypass and the 4 not affected; the 4 unaffected sites give a cleaner (if small) estimate of the camera effect.
Look at severity (killed or seriously injured vs slight), since speed reductions are expected to reduce severity more than frequency; even a modest 3 mph fall in mean speed may matter there.

question: How much did the smaller default chip portion with free refills reduce chip waste, and should the change be rolled out across the restaurant group?
data:
One restaurant branch. From week 5, the default portion of chips served with mains was reduced and free refills were offered on request. Weeks 1-4 (before) vs weeks 5-8 (after):

| | Weeks 1-4 | Weeks 5-8 |
| Covers (meals served) | 2,400 | 2,000 |
| Chip plate waste, weighed at the wash-up station | 360 kg | 210 kg |
| Chips purchased (frozen) | 1,200 kg | 900 kg |
| Customer satisfaction (mean score, 1-5) | 4.4 | 4.3 |
| Complaints about portion size | 2 | 11 |

Kitchen note: from week 5, refill chips that were cooked but not served (for example, cooked for a refill request that was then declined, or left in the fryer basket at close) were thrown into the kitchen general-waste bin, not weighed at the wash-up station. Kitchen staff estimate this at 40 kg over weeks 5-8. Before week 5 there were no refills, and kitchen chip waste was negligible.

Chip cost: £1.20 per kg (frozen).

The group has 12 branches. Menus differ: 5 branches do not serve chips with mains.
draft:
**Chip portion trial: waste and cost results**

**What changed.** From week 5 the default chip portion was reduced and free refills were offered on request. This note compares weeks 1-4 with weeks 5-8 at one branch, 4,400 covers in total. We report three measures: plate waste per cover, chips purchased per cover, and customer feedback.

**Waste.** Measured at the wash-up station, chip waste fell from 360 kg to 210 kg over four weeks, 150 kg less in absolute terms. Because the restaurant served fewer covers in the second period (2,000 against 2,400), the fair comparison is waste per cover. Before the change, plate waste was 150 g per cover (360 kg / 2,400). After the change it was 95 g per cover, a 37% reduction.

**Purchasing.** Chip purchases fell from 1,200 kg to 900 kg. Purchases cover chips for both the main portion and refills. Total purchases fell by 300 kg, or 25%. Per cover, that is a fall from 0.50 kg to 0.45 kg, which at £1.20 per kg saves 6p per cover. On 2,000 covers per four weeks, that is about £120 per four-week period, or roughly £1,560 a year for the branch.

**Customers.** Customer satisfaction moved only slightly, from 4.4 to 4.3 on the restaurant's usual five-point scale, and complaints about portion size remained negligible. Customers who want more can ask for a refill.

**Environmental benefit.** Less food waste means less waste sent for disposal and lower emissions from the food we buy but do not use. Buying less food in the first place is the most direct way to cut waste. The trial shows that a simple, low-cost change in portioning can make a real difference.

**Rollout.** The change is simple to implement and requires no new equipment. Rolling the change out to all 12 branches should cut chip waste by over a third across the group, delivering similar savings in every branch. Branches would need a short briefing on the new portion standard and how to offer refills, and each should weigh plate waste weekly for the first two months.

**Recommendation.** Roll out the smaller default portion with free refills to all branches from next month, and continue weighing plate waste at the wash-up station to track results. The change needs only a revised portion standard and a process for serving refills to order. We also suggest recording refills on the till system so that we can see how often customers ask for more.

flaws.location: After the change it was 95 g per cover, a 37% reduction
flaws.description: 210 kg / 2,000 covers = 105 g per cover, not 95 g.
flaws.correction: 105 g per cover, a 30% reduction in plate waste per cover.

flaws.location: Measured at the wash-up station, chip waste fell from 360 kg to 210 kg over four weeks
flaws.description: Ignores the kitchen note: after the change, about 40 kg of cooked but unserved refill chips went into general waste and were not weighed. Before the change, kitchen chip waste was negligible.
flaws.correction: Total chip waste after = 250 kg, or 125 g per cover: a 17% reduction (125 vs 150 g), not 30% or 37%.

flaws.location: complaints about portion size remained negligible
flaws.description: Complaints about portion size rose from 2 to 11 (from about 0.8 to 5.5 per 1,000 covers).
flaws.correction: Portion complaints rose more than fivefold, a real customer cost to weigh against the savings.

flaws.location: Rolling the change out to all 12 branches should cut chip waste by over a third across the group
flaws.description: Generalises one branch's four-week result to all branches, including 5 that do not serve chips with mains. It also relies on the inflated waste figure.
flaws.correction: At most, a similar effect might be expected in the 7 branches that serve chips with mains, and only after a longer trial; the per-cover reduction is about 17% once kitchen waste is included.

open_extensions: Use purchasing as an independent check: chip purchases per cover fell 10% (0.50 to 0.45 kg), which bounds the real change in chips used and is consistent with a modest, not dramatic, reduction in waste.

Extend the trial and add a comparison branch: four weeks per period is short, and covers fell 17% between periods, so a concurrent control branch would separate the portion effect from seasonal or menu-mix changes.
Weigh kitchen chip waste separately from now on, so that the full waste stream (plate + kitchen) is measured in any rollout.

question: How much did the SMS reminder scheme reduce missed appointments (no-shows) at the GP practice, and what is it worth per quarter?
data:
GP practice. From 1 January, an SMS reminder is sent two days before every appointment booked more than 3 days in advance. Appointments booked 3 days ahead or less get no reminder.

| Period | Booking lead time | Appointments | No-shows |
| Oct-Dec (before) | More than 3 days ahead | 2,400 | 312 |
| Oct-Dec (before) | 3 days or less | 3,600 | 228 |
| Jan-Mar (after) | More than 3 days ahead (SMS sent) | 3,200 | 160 |
| Jan-Mar (after) | 3 days or less (no SMS) | 3,200 | 288 |

Totals: before, 6,000 appointments and 540 no-shows; after, 6,400 appointments and 448 no-shows.

Operations log: on 3 days in November the practice phone system failed, so patients could not call to cancel or rebook. The practice attributes 120 of the before-period no-shows in the 'more than 3 days ahead' group to those 3 days. No other disruptions occurred in either period.

Cost per SMS: 4p. The practice estimates that each no-show costs £30 in wasted clinician time.
draft:
**SMS reminders: effect on missed appointments**

**Background.** Since 1 January the practice has sent an SMS reminder two days before every appointment booked more than 3 days ahead. This note estimates the effect on no-shows and the value to the practice. It compares October-December (before) with January-March (after), split by how far ahead each appointment was booked. Appointments rose from 6,000 to 6,400 between the two quarters.

**Overall change.** The no-show rate fell from 9.0% (540 of 6,000) in October-December to 7.0% (448 of 6,400) in January-March. No-shows fell from 540 to 448, 92 fewer, even though there were 400 more appointments. That is a fall of 2 percentage points, a 29% reduction in the no-show rate.

**By booking lead time.** Among appointments booked more than 3 days ahead, the group that receives reminders, the rate fell from 13.0% to 5.0%. For appointments booked 3 days or less ahead, which receive no reminder, the rate rose from 6.3% to 9.0%. Both groups are large, with at least 2,400 appointments in each period. However, comparing all appointments before and after is the simplest fair test of the reminders, because it captures the practice-wide effect and avoids slicing the data into smaller groups. I therefore use the overall figures for the headline estimate.

**Appointments recovered.** A 2-point fall applied to 6,400 appointments a quarter means about 128 fewer no-shows per quarter.

**Value.** Each no-show costs the practice an estimated £50 in wasted clinician time, so 128 fewer no-shows are worth about £6,400 per quarter. Against this, the SMS cost is small: 3,200 reminders at 4p each, £128 a quarter, or about £1 per no-show avoided. The scheme therefore returns about fifty times its cost. Over a year, the saving would be about £25,600.

**Why did the short-notice rate rise?** The rise in no-shows among short-notice appointments is unexpected. It may reflect winter illness, since January to March is a busy period, but we cannot tell from these data.

**Recommendation.** Continue the SMS scheme, and consider extending reminders to appointments booked 2-3 days ahead, sent the day before. No-show rates should be reported monthly, split by booking lead time, so that the effect can be tracked, and the scheme should be reviewed again after a full year. Reminders also give patients a prompt to cancel if they no longer need the appointment, which frees the slot for someone else. The comparison is between two consecutive quarters, so seasonal differences between autumn and winter may affect both groups.

flaws.location: a 29% reduction in the no-show rate
flaws.description: A fall from 9.0% to 7.0% is 2/9 = 22% in relative terms, not 29%.
flaws.correction: A 22% relative reduction (on the overall figures).

flaws.location: comparing all appointments before and after is the simplest fair test of the reminders
flaws.description: The overall comparison mixes the treated group with an untreated group whose share of appointments changed (40% of appointments before were booked more than 3 days ahead, 50% after) and whose rate moved for other reasons. The effect should be estimated in the group that received reminders.
flaws.correction: Use the 'more than 3 days ahead' group: 13.0% to 5.0%, 8 points × 3,200 = 256 fewer no-shows a quarter on the unadjusted figures (but see the omission flaw).

flaws.location: the rate fell from 13.0% to 5.0%
flaws.description: Ignores the phone-system failure, which the practice says caused 120 of the before-period no-shows in exactly this group.
flaws.correction: Adjusted before rate: (312 − 120) / 2,400 = 8.0%. Reminder effect: 8.0% to 5.0%, 3 points, about 96 fewer no-shows a quarter on 3,200 appointments.

flaws.location: Each no-show costs the practice an estimated £50 in wasted clinician time
flaws.description: The practice's estimate is £30 per no-show, not £50.
flaws.correction: At £30: 96 × £30 = about £2,880 per quarter against £128 of SMS costs (about 22 times the cost).

open_extensions: Use the short-notice group as a rough control for background change: its rate rose 2.7 points (6.3% to 9.0%). If that background rise also applied to longer-lead bookings, the reminder effect would be larger than 3 points; state the bounds rather than a single figure.
Check the change in booking mix: the share of appointments booked more than 3 days ahead rose from 40% to 50%. Ask whether reminders, or a change in booking policy, drove this.
Recommend a cleaner test, e.g. randomising reminders for a few weeks, or comparing with a neighbouring practice without SMS, to separate the reminder effect from seasonal change.
